Before the Orders of the day are called, I would like to bring to the attention of the government a telegram which I received late on Friday afternoon. It is as follows :
Fort Frances, Ont., July 16.
R. L. Borden,
Ottawa.
Canadian Northern has daily passenger trains east and west. Spite this, mail for Rainy River valley comes by freight and is practically suspended. People are using American mail, express boats to Rat Portage, and any available means to forward mail out, but have had only one mail in for past seven days. Business is paralyzed, and we can get no relief from Post Office Department. If this is economy, it means at a ruinous cost to a growing and ambitious district. Please help us.
W. J. KEATING, Mayor.
I know nothing of the circumstances, and the only course open to me was to bring this matter to the attention of the government at the earliest possible moment.

With reference to the subject of mail service at Fort Frances, to which the hon. leader of the opposition, has alluded, when this subject was brought to my attention two or three days ago, I applied to the comptroller of the railway mail service for an explanation. He informed me that the service between Winnipeg and Fort Frances was performed by the Canadian Northern Railway, by their regular train service, which at that time was limited to three trains per week. I think the days were Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. Without the consent of the department, the railway company decided to discontinue the running of that train service as heretofore regularly to Fort Frances, but to stop at same point west, and intended, in lieu thereof, to put on an express train. The express train as I am informed was not established for a few days after Friday, the last regular day of the local to which I have referred. Accordingly there was a hiatus cused by this change in the running of the train. The moment the matter was called to my attention, instructions were given to utilize all the trains, which is now being done. Of course it is the privilege of the mayor to write as he likes to a member of the House and for an hon. member to read his telegram, but it is quite an unfair way of presenting the case.
Mr, BORDEN (Halifax). I do not know whether my hon. friend intends to charge me with any unfairness.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Muloclt).

speechtext: If my hon. friend had submitted the telegram to me, I could have shown him that the- reasons assigned were without foundation.

On the Order for :
The second reading of the amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 150, to incorporate the Columbia River Improvement Company, Limited.
Mr. GALLIHER moved that the said amendment be amended by striking out the words ' section seven ' in the second amendment and inserting instead thereof 'sections seven and eight.' He said : It is Inexpedient to include section seven unless section eight is also included, as section eight covers waters not mentioned in section seven. The Senate, in section fourteen, proposed the following amendment : After the word ' operate,' in the first line, they wish to insert ' on the waters mentioned in section 7 hereof.' That would make the section read : ' The company may acquire and operate, on the waters mentioned in section 7 hereof, the works of any company having powers wholly or in part similar to the powers of the company.' Now, that would only give this company the privilege of acquiring the works of other companies at a point on the shores of Upper Arrow lake, or at a point on Upper Arrow lake where the Columbia river enters it, but would not give the powers which they require of acquiring works of other companies that might construct works upon the Columbia river above Upper Arrow lake or upon navigable tributaries of the Columbia river. Evidently the Senate did not notice that there were different points asked for as covered in section 7 and section 8. By inserting the words ' sections 7 and 8 ' we cover the waters mentioned In these sections, and the company would acquire what they really ask for* and what is necessary in their interest.

I understand, then, that in this section, as it was at first the provision was general, but the Senate has limited it to the point referred to in section 7. Section 8 is a companion section to section 7. and, if it is restricted, you should refer to both these sections.

" Yes, that is it.
Amendment, as amended, agreed to.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 224) to amend the Fisheries Act, was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
The section substituted for section 6 of the Fisheries Act, chapter 95 of the revised statutes, by section 1 of chapter 51 of the statutes of 1894. is repealed, and -the following is substituted therefor :-
6.	Every one w-ho hunts or kills fish or marine animals of any kind, other than seals, porpoises, whales and walruses, by means of rockets, explosive materials, or explosive projectiles or shells, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding three hundred dollars and costs, and, in default of payment, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.
What change is effected in the law by this section ?

At the present time there is no pnwer in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to allow any of the animals here designated to lie killed with explosives. Under this amendment. permission may be given to hunt and kill seals, porpoises, whales and walruses with explosives, explosive projectiles and so on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speechtext: What is the rea. son of making that change ?

Requests have been received that licenses be issued in certain parts of our waters to establish whaling stations; to be conducted on modern lines, that is to say, as they are conducted in other countries, with the use of explosives. The department thought the Canadian fishermen should be placed in the same position as the fishermen of other countries. So on the recommendation of the commissioner of fisheries it has been decided to ask for the necessary power to amend the law to that effect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is it the usual custom of fishermen in other countries to use explosives ?
In other countries it is, but in this country, so far, it has not been allowed.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
This industry is largely engaged in Newfoundland. They use this method of throwing the harpoons and killing the whales.
On section 3,

This is the result of the Investigation which has been held in British Columbia, and it has been recommended that we should allow purse seines to be used under special license in the waters of the Pacific coast. The question of traps has been left in abeyance in the meantime, so no mention is made in the Bill of traps. All we require at the present time is an amendment which will enable the department to allow special licenses to issue in British Columbia waters for the use of purse seines, in accordance with the almost unanimous opinion of those engaged in that industry.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If persons are to be prohibited from this method of fishing in the Atlantic waters, why are they to be allowed in the Pacific waters ?

It is thought proper to allow it in British Columbia waters because the Americans are using the same mode of fishing. It has been established
by those who have studied the question that it is the best mode of catching fish in these waters, and it is the most profitable way of carrying on that industry alongside of our American cousins, who are practising it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: When the same methods were employed in the Atlantic, they were found an injury to the fish, and when our government approached the United States government asking them to abolish that method they consented to do so. I think the same thing should be asked for in the Pacific waters, and I think it would be granted by the American government ; otherwise, in the course of a little while the fish will become extinct.

For the information of the hon. member I may state that though this question is new to me, it is not new to the department, where it has been studied for the last three years. Voluminous correspondence has been had with the American authorities in the matter, and they have refused point blank to concede anything in the line of abolishing purse seines. They have gone further and they have established traps. At the same time they are taking so many salmon witli these traps that it has become a very serious question in British Columbia whether within a year or two we should not also allow traps as tlie Americans are using them. But some of the parties interested in tlie fishing industry were not ready to go so far as to use traps, and they unanimously recommended that purse seines should be allowed to be used. At present the industry is threatened with great injury, and is liable to be seriously diminished if the Department of Fisheries is not allowed to license purse seines.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) At present American seiners are frequenting the coast of Nova Scotia in the spring of the year with their purse seines, and take every opportunity of catching mackerel outside tlie three-mile limit, and inside the three-mile limit, unless our own steamers are there to prevent them. Now, it would be considered something of a hardship if our own fishermen within the three-mile limit were not able to use the same method of catching mackerel as the Americans enjoy outside the three-mile limit. If we could only get the American government to abolisli purse seines altogether, then it would be a mutual advantage to prevent entirely that method of catching mackerel. But at present the American fishermen will enjoy a privilege on our own coast that, by this Bill, will be denied to our own fishermen. I know of several merchants in Halifax who are in the possession of very expensive purse seines at present.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was not aware that any privilege was allowed Americans on the shores of Nova Scotia inside the three mile limit.
No.

I quite understand what the hon. member said, but i was not aware that they were permitted outside the three-mile limit, though it may be that they may have the seines on board clandestinely, and may catcli mackerel in that way. But if sucli is the case, I tuink it would be advisable for the government to communicate with the American government and ask them to abolish trap seines entirely, and to see that tneir fleet are not permitted to employ that metliou of fishing. I will go further and say that if the Americans persist in using purse seines in the waters of the Atlantic, then we should match them with a similar method. We did catch large quantities at one time with purse seines, hut we found that they destroyed the fish and we gave it up entirely. As I said before, the Americans consented to do the same.
They have not done so, I am informed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Our government should approach the American government again and ask them to abolish that method of fishing.

Before issuing these licenses I may take the precaution of corresponding witli the American authorities in the matter. and informing them that we have now the power to license this method of fishing and intend to do so unless they will stop it on their side; if they do not, then we will proceed under this law.
I am only referring to purse seines.

Under what conditions do you propose to authorize the use of purse seines in Rritish Columbia waters?

speechtext: I think before the minister should take upon himself to interdict entirely the use of purse seines in our waters, on the erroneous grounds, ns I think, that they are seriously diminishing the mackerel, it would be well for the department to make an examination into the whole matter. I wish to tell the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if he will turn to the report made to the London Fisheries Commission of 1883, by Prof Huxley, Sir John Lubbock, and another gentleman whose name I forget, he will learn that they lay it down that man is powerless practically to diminish deep sea fish by any means he may use to exterminate them. These professors came to this conclusion after a most complete examination of the conditions surrounding the fisheries of the North Sea and the German Ocean for from 50 to 200 years. It was pointed out that tlie mackerel will leave our coasts tinder certain conditions because the food they feed upon disappears, that the foot! disappears because certain vegetation disappears, and that the vegetation disappears because certain currents are changed. If that is so, I think it is scarcely worth while for the government to listen to folk lore in reference to this matter. It would be far better to examine into the matter scientifically and arrive at a conclusion that will have a solid basis before any action is taken. I have observed the fisheries on the Atlantic coast for some years. I know that in 1889 more mackerel re-appeared on the Nova Scotian coast than probably have ever been caught by mankind in the history of the world. The same thing occurred last year.
They reappeared in considerable numbers since then, did they not-in 1899, or thereabouts ?
I do not know about 1S99, but they came in last year.

They reappeared last year in larger numbers than usual. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) says that they appear every year, but not in such large numbers as they did last year. The main object of the prevention of the use of purse seines in Atlantic waters was that the Americans would come, together with some of our own vessels, and capture fish outside

of the three-mile limit, thus preventing those who fish in competition with them from the shore, from getting a catch at all, because, the moment purse seines are used outside of the three-mile limit, in deep water the fish will disappear altogether. They are driven away from the shore and they will not reappear again during the season. _
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I decidedly object to allowing the Americans a privilege on our coast that cannot be enjoyed by our own fishermen. The Ameri-' cans will come, as they did this spring, and take home large cargoes of mackerel caught off the coast of Nova Scotia in their purse seines. They will always take advantage of the opportunity of coming within the three-mile limit whenever there is not one of our own cruisers on the coast to prevent them. There is no doubt that they adopt that method of poaching whenever' they get the opportunity. Our own people have purse seines and they sometimes prosecute the mackerel fishery in that way. 1 do not think that there is any chance of any correspondence that may take place with the American government being effective as to the prohibition of the use of purse seines. They have too much interest and too much money invested in vessels and seines employed in the catching of fish to listen to anything that can be said by our government against their present method of catching mackerel. I think it is quite a hardship just now that we should prevent our own fishermen from adopting the same method that the Americans enjoy at the present time, because, I know that there are firms in Halifax which have purse seines and vessels to prosecute the fishery and it would be quite a hardship to adopt any law by which we should prevent them from enjoying the privilege which hitherto they have enjoyed.

Would the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) kindly repeat the last question which he put to the hon. minister ? I confess I did not quite grasp the point of it nor yet the answer of the hon. minister.

I wanted to learn from the hon. minister what would be the conditions under which licenses would be issued, and I understood from the hon. minister's reply that they would be issued under certain regulations prepared by the department here, and that all who applied under these regulations would without discrimination have licenses issued to them, that there would be no discrimination in the issue of licenses to all who complied with the regulations of the department. Am I correct in so understanding the hon. minister?

They would have to conform with the regulations. The regulations will
probably determine how many licenses will be issued for a certain space. We cannot pile them one upon another. It depends necessarily on what will be the recommendation of those who know exactly how this law will work out. Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) does not expect the department to grant licenses at random. The regulations would have to provide for the territory where the applicants are allowed to fish. This is a special way of fishing and these purse seines are very large. The regulations would have to provide that so many purse seines may be used within a certain space.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does the department propose to issue these purse seine licenses to a limited number of people and to discriminate against other people who may make application for them ? Do I understand that the hon. minister will determine from amongst the number of applicants for permission to use purse seines who shall be permitted to use them and who shall not be permitted to use them ?
I never said anything of the kind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is what the hon. minister has been saying all the time.

Then, I was misunderstood. I am not posted enough on the question to tell the committee what the regulations will be, but the regulations will be decided by the officers having regard to the practice in other countries where purse seines are authorized, and I suppose the regulations would provide for the use of so many purse seines within, say, a distance of fifty miles, because, it is impossible to have more than that number and, of course, those who apply first and who can fulfil the conditions will get the preference. I do not see how we could do otherwise. I suppose that one of the regulations which has been enforced by the department for a couple of years will be continued and that is the regulation providing that there shall be no speculation in licenses. Licenses cannot be transferred without the authority of the department. Otherwise, there might be cases where ten or twenty persons might club together, get the licenses for a certain space and sell them. It is not the intention to permit such speculation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
1 do not know enough about the methods of fishing on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts to be able to form an opinion of much value, but it strikes me that if the hon. minister is authorized to issue these purse seine licenses to certain persons and to say who shall be permitted to use these purse seines that this proposition may be liable to grave abuse. If there are twenty persons engaged in fishing in a certain district and the hon. minister
69fi.fi

says that the territory is not wide enough to permit more than ten to prosecute the fishery, how will lie discriminate as between those who are to be allowed to fish with purse seines and those who are not allowed to fish with purse seines ?
The same way as we determine how many lobster licenses shall be granted in a certain district.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Who does determine who gets them ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND I 1 HERIES. The officer in charge. It has been the custom to give the preference to the one who used to own the license. Sometimes it has been decided to increase the number and sometimes to decrease it, but the people are notified and nobody is taken by surprise.
Some body is taken by surprise if twenty apply and only ten are granted licenses.
That, of course, is unavoidable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am Inclined to think that the minister has taken quite a burden upon his shoulders, and lie will have difficulty in discriminating as to who are to receive licensfs and who are not.
It is the same in all other wa ters.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: With regard to cur own waters I want to be understood as saying that if the Americans are allowed to operate with purse seines in the catch of mackerel or other fish, then our fishermen should be allowed to do likewise. Of course, if we could restrict the Americans from purse seining, I would wish to have some such arrangement made as was formerly in effect. My hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) says that they do catch fish with purse seines inside the three-mile limit, which means that they poach. If that is the case, it is all the greater reason for the government to have more patrol vessels on the coast to prevent such poaching. It is a serious matter when the shore fishermen find Americans coining down with fifty and sixty in a fleet and depleting the waters of fish, while our Canadians inshore are unable in their small boats to capture any. Therefore, I would say that some arrangement should be made by which we could place ourselves in an equal position with the Americans as regards the capture of fisli.
Is there anything in this Bill which prevents Canadian fishermen from fishing with purse seines outside the three-mile limit.
Nothing whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then, if that be the case, American fishermen have no privileges that Canadian fishermen do not enjoy. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbacli) appears to be under the impression that American fishermen have some privileges which our own fishermen have not.
Not at all. The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. We have no jurisdiction outside of the three mile limit.
We have the same rights that other fishermen have.
We cannot control the Americans outside of that three mile limit, but what I complain of is that the Americans take the right to themselves inside the three mile limit.

That is poaching, and I would be glad to see the fishery protection service made as efficient as possible so as to stop that. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) referred to reports made by certain professors to the effect that no device yet known to man could diminish the number and quantity of fisli In the waters. Well, I hardly think that is correct even though celebrated professors are responsible for the statement. Fact is more important than theory, and the fact is that since purse seining was introduced the mackerel on our Atlantic coast in Canadian waters have been very greatly reduced and our fishermen do not now make the profits they formerly made. While fishing was done by hand-line, and before the days of purse seining, the industry was a very certain one. The fishermen fitted out their ships and boats and they were almost certain to return with a profitable fare, but since purse seining lias been introduced it has become a most precarious business, and the shore fishermen at least are most frequently doomed to failure. If any international arrangement could be made by which purse seining would be abolished, it would, in my opinion, be the very best thing that could be done. Of course, we cannot prevent the Americans from fishing outside of the three mile limit, and failing an International agreement, the only thing we Canadians can do is to protect the inshore fisheries in the best possible way. Purse seining is most destruc-11 \ e to fish life. The seine incloses a large quantity of small mackerel and other small fish which are thrown overboard to foul the bottom and frighten the fisli off the coast. The mackerel in some way are supposed to know when they are chased by seiners, and it is the opinion of men of long experience in the business that they abandon the coast when they are so pursued. As I have said, the best thing would be an international

arrangement to abolish purse seining, but failing that the next best thing is for us to protect our own fishermen as best we can within the three mile limit.

Is this Bill intended to apply principally to British Columbia ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AN1>
FISHERIES. Yes.

Has the minister taken into consideration that the Americans are both using purse seining and trap nets along the great lakes and on the international rivers. It appears to me that the object of this Bill is rather to imitate the bad example of the Americans than to provide a solution for the difficulty. The trouble with regard to the great lakes and rivers that divide Canada from the United States is just as great as that which the minister endeavours to provide for in this Bill f r British Columbia. Do I understand that the minister will issue licenses under certain regulations for purse and trap net fishing on the great lakes, or whether the intention is to confine the provisions of this Bill entirely to British Columbia ?

This Bill applies only to the British Columbia waters. It is the result of several years of special study that has been made of the question out there, and the people have come to a unanimous co.u-clusion upon it. I do not think that the conditions are the same on the great lakes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The Americans are using purse seines and trap nets on the great lakes.
The MINISTER OF MARINE ANI) FISHERIES. Trap nets are allowed.
Do I understand the minister to say that his department issues regulations governing the number of licenses on the great lakes ?
We have not done so as yet, but it might be opportune to do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understand that the Ontario government have the right to control the fisheries in the inland waters. That being true, they would have to say how many licenses shall be issued.
The Dominion government controls the regulations, and the licenses are issued by the Ontario government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Therefore, this government have no control over the number of licenses that are issued ?
They might do so by regulations. They have not done so yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think there is some misapprehension between the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and the minister in regard to the regulation pertaining to provincial licenses for purse seines, as proposed to be issued. I do not understand the minister to say that so many of these licenses shall be issued for certain sections, say within twenty miles or within fifty miles.
That is what the minister said.

I think the minister must have misunderstood the hon. gentleman. If he did say that, I think he must have had in his mind the recommendations of the superintendent of fisheries in the province of British Columbia, Mr. Babcock, -who, I believe, has recommended to the Department of Marine and Fisheries here that if the government ever issued purse seine licenses, they should be confined to certain designated districts. Speaking for myself, and I represent that part of the province of British Columbia which is perhaps most interested in the fisheries there-I think that there are the strongest and most cogent reasons why that should not be done, but that, if these licenses are Issued, say in New Westminster, the licensees should be permitted to go and fish in the waters of the Skeena river or in any other waters of British Columbia. Two years ago a commission was appointed, of which I was a member, to look into this matter and to make recommendations to the government, and one of its recommendations was that these purse seine licenses be issued. It deprecated the issue of licenses for traps.
I believe that the government decided not to issue licenses for traps, notwithstanding the rumours to the contrary, but that they decided to issue purse seine licenses, and with no restriction as to locality.
Are we to understand, then, that all who comply with the regulations which may. from time to time, be adopted and published by the department may procure these purse seine licenses ?

That is certainly what I strongly advocate, and what I think, from my rather limited knowledge of these matters, though I have made some study of them, is the best policy to adopt ; though there will have to be regulations regulating those who get the licenses. There may be some to whom they would be worthless. Under a salmon license, for instance, which any man can get on paying $10, there are certain regulations which make it unlawful for one man to fish within a certain distance of another. That would limit the number of licenses issued for certain waters. But there would be no discrimination ; each one would have to take his chance. I think complications would be avoided if purse seine licenses were issued without restric-

tion as to the locality where the licensees might fish.
What is the mode of fishing with these purse seines 1 Is it done from a vessel ?

Not necessarily from the vessel ; they may be attached to the tug boat. They are not attached to the shore, and they are not permitted in what are known as closed waters-the estuaries of rivers, bays, runs, passes, and inlets of that kind. I understand that it is the intention, as it is the proper thing, to prohibit fishing in these narrow or closed waters. This step on the part of the government seems to be due to the methods adopted by the Americans, who fish south of the international line without any restriction whatever, every hour of the day, and every day of the week, and by every method they can invent, while immediately across the international boundary line the Dominion government imposes certain restrictions upon the licensees, such as forty-eight hours of close season.	4
As a result, the Canadian fishermen get the worst of it, do they not ?

I think that complaint is not well founded. If Canadians were permitted to fish with traps in the outside waters where the salmon are, it is supposed that they would break up this trap fishing by the Americans ; but that is only a conjecture. An ordinary fisherman could not take advantage of a trap net; it is too cumbersome and involves too large an expenditure. But the purse seine is comparatively inexpensive, and two or three or half a dozen fishermen could club together and go out and invade the territory of these Americans w'ho are fishing by the trap methods, and relieve the difficulty in that respect. The people on the coast of British Columbia think that something should be done other than the gill-net method of fishing by the Canadians ; but they are not prepared to go to the extent of asking to have trap nets ; and this provision is a kind of compromise which may be very effective, and may conduce to the development of the fishing industry in British Columbia.
I understand that the regulations of the department will not discriminate against anybody, but that all who comply with them will have licenses issued to them ?

That is What we strongly impressed on the minister, so that I suspect that the minister must have misunderstood the hon. member when he asked that question, and had in mind the strong recommendation made by the superintendent of fisheries in British Columbia. Although he is a very capable man, his experience has been on the south side of the line, and he is very anxious to see traps introduced,
which I think would be a most Improper and indefensible policy for the government to adopt. I rather think the minister must have had that in his mind.
When was that V

This spring. I am only addressing the House to endorse the remarks of my hon. friend from Cape Breton. To say that the mackerel are going to be depleted by any method we can use to catch them is absurd. The quantity we take in fishing on the coast of Nova Scotia or Scotland is only a drop in the bucket, considering the quantity to be found in these waters year after year. 1 read an article recently on herring fishing on the coast of Scotland, in which this statement was made, that there are more herring destroyed and eaten by the gannets and other sea birds on the coast of Scotland during the year than are taken by the fishermen, and it is well known that the herring fishing on the coast of Scotland is the largest in the world. The fish follow the bait, and if they do not frequent our shores as usual from year to year, it is because they have not the bait there which they generally follow. The deep cod-fishing on the banks of Newfoundland and St. Pierre and all along there is increasing in spite of the catch from year to year, and in spite of the length of time these fisheries have been exploited. First the Portuguse, then the Spaniards, then the Frenchmen, and lastly our own people have prosecuted that industry, and whenever our fishermen are successful in getting the proper bait the fish is as abundant as ever. To say that we are going to destroy our fisheries by the quantity we are going to catch is an old woman's story.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he would accept an amendment to make the meaning more clear of subsection 8, of section 8. The subsection reads 4 No one shall drift for salmon except in British Columbia ' and the amendment I would suggest is to strike out the words ' drift for salmon ' and insert instead ' catch salmon with drift-net.' The reason is that parties say that they are not drifting for salmon but for other fish, and if they catch salmon they cannot help it. They thus seek to evade the law although their object is to catch salmon. While on my feet. I would also like to draw attention to subsection 7 of section 14.	' No one shall
use drag-net, bag-net, trap-net, pound-net or fish-weir of any kind, without a special license, for the capture of deep sea fish, other than salmon.' I want to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the expression ' trap-net ' which has created great trouble in Nova Scotia. In some parts of the province, on the south, the fisheries officers are exacting a license fee for a certain net. which they claim to be a trap-net, but in other parts they are not because they say it is not a trap-net. The whole point of contention seems to be that one set of officers say that a net, in order to be a trap-net. must have a net floor, and that that
constitutes the distinction between a trap-net and another kind of net, whereas others contend that any net which operates as a trap to catch fish is a trap-net. It is important that an interpretation should be placed on the term ' trap-net.'
The fishermen on the shore in some localities, in days gone by, fished with a seine which they shot out from the shore around the school of mackerel. But, in later years, they put out a seine from the shore, and construct at the end of it what they call a bowl, which is in the shape of an arrowhead, or circular, with a leader from the mouth of said bowl. The mackerel coming down the shore strike the leaders and are led into the bowl where they are easily inclosed. Nets of that description, I believe, are without a floor in most localities. What was originally meant to come within the designation of a trap net within the Act was constructed on the principle of setting out stakes planted firmly on the bottom and nets strung along the stakes, and then a floor put in, so that there was no way the fish could get out at all. But it is unfortunate that the law as it stands at the present moment is in such a form that one judge may decide that a certain net is a trap-net and another may decide that it is not a trap-net. I think it would be well to have an interpretation. But for the present I would ask the minister to accept the amendment I have proposed.
The hon. member's (Mr. Wade) amendment may involve a difficulty of interpretation. For instance, on the Fraser river
It does not apply to that.

But it might apply to waters where the circumstances are similar. Obviously you could not have a drift-net except in a current. All these nets are regulated as to mesh, and there is no difference between a drift-net and another net except in the use of it. It is a drift-net because it is thrown into running water and it drifts. They may not tie it to the shore. Or it might be permanent and tied to the shore.
That would be a drift-net.
I am not sure.
A drift-net is not a net attached to the shore or to a buoy.

But the name applies to the method of fishing rather than to the net. You have a drift-net by virtue of the fact that you fish in running water, and that distinguishes that method of fishing from the permanent method of fishing.

I would like to ask the minister whether or not there has been a report of the committee with regard

to certain matters mentioned in this Bill V I think the hon. minister was good enough to say, when the Bill was introduced, that he would lay a copy of the report upon tiie Table, so that we might consider it when we came to discuss the Bill in committee.

I said I would give the substance of what the report purports to be. I do not know why it has not been laid on the Table. But the result of the investigation was, purely and simply to recommend what is in the Bill as respects purse seines.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: To meet the suggestion of my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Matlie-son) I would change the form of my amendment to read ' no person shall drift for or catch salmon with a drift-net.' This will allow for the exception of British Columbia.

I think it is possible to make too many laws. I have been connected with the fisheries for the last forty years, from a time when the government did not interfere with the fishing at all, except in the rivers. The catch of mackerel during the present season is as big as it was forty years ago. It is well enough to make laws to regulate the fisheries in rivers and inland waters, but, as to the fishing in the Atlantic, you may interfere with the subject, but you cannot interfere with the fish-not a bit. Providence furnishes too many fish for your little attempts to interfere with them. There is such a thing as governing people too much. To undertake to make regulations for the fishing in the Atlantic is entirely unnecessary. We might be better employed. And I may say that it does not seem to be thoroughly understood what a drift-net is. It ought to be considered the same here as in the old country. A fisherman goes out in his boat in the evening, ties a net to his boat and drifts all night, returning with his catch in the morning. That is not surrounding the fish, but simply giving the fish a chance to get into the net.

We seem to be dealing with two things at the same time.
I wish to confine myself to section 3, of the Bill. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Morrison) has apparently taken a different view of conditions that should be imposed from that which the Minister of Marine takes. The minister seems to be under the impression that there is to be a territorial limit to these purse seines. From what I have been able to gather and from what I previously knew as to the nature of the purse seines, I do not see how that is possible. The minister likens it to a license for a lobster factory. But the license for a purse seine is different; it is a license to take the purse seine and go out on the river or the ocean at the mouth of a river and use the purse seine to catch Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
fish. If I am not right in my understanding, perhaps my hon. friend will say so.
Yes, with a variation.

Well, that is the way they are used in the Atlantic, they put them on board their vessels and take them out. If that is the case, how are you to regulate territorial limits where these purse seines are used on the Pacific coasts ? I would think with the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. Morrison) that you should give the license to any person who applies, subject perhaps to certain conditions in the way of user. For example, if some one is using a purse seine at the mouth of the Fraser river, another man must not run his purse seines across those of the first man, or do anything that would prevent a legitimate use of them by the man who was first occupying that position. No man should take up a territorial limit and be able to say, that belongs to me, to the exclusion o>f every one else. I do not see that the question of territory can have anything to do with it. I gathered from the minister that there would be some question of territorial limit with regard to the user.
There were recommendations to that effect, but we have come to no decision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: So far as I am concerned, I would be inclined to protest against any regulation of that kind. You may make a regulation as to the way in which a man should use his purse seines on the river, at the same time preventing him from doing detriment to any one else.
He would use it in the open water, not at the mouth of the river.
The mouth of the river is twelve or fifteen miles wide, is it not ?
That would scarcely be called a river, but the point is to prevent them going into the estuaries or closed waters of any kind.

The hon. gentleman is more familiar with the circumstances than I am. But subject to that, I would repeat the view I have expressed, and what the member for New Westminster has said about it would emphasize my view, that you cannot have any question of territorial limit. The only regulations of any use would be those which prevented one man from interfering with the use of purse seines by another man. If the minister would give us a little more definite idea of what conditions he intends to impose, it would enable us to discuss the matter more intelligently.

It is impossible at present to

say what the conditions will be, as we will require to study the matter carefully before framing regulations in order to make them fair and reasonable to all parties concerned. At present there is some disagreement between the parties interested, and we shall have to consult them before framing the regulations.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is there any intention to confine the issue of these licenses to political friends, and to withhold them from political opponents ?
There may be no political opponents out there.
Since I have been in the department so far, I have made no distinction on political grounds between applicants. They will all be treated fairly.

speechtext: In view of the fact that the minister desires to have an opportunity further to consider my amendment to this Bill, I will not press it, but I will ask him to take the matter into consideration during the recess with the view of interpreting those words ' trap net.' Perhaps this session he will be able to introduce a further amendment to interpret those words. It is important to do so, because there is a great deal of litigation going on at the present time in consequence of doubt as to the meaning of those words, and that litigation is likely to increase.

I will with pleasure look into it.

, The MINISTER OF FINANCE. My attention has occasionally been drawn to the ease of mutilated silver. speechtext: Bill (No. 179) to amend the Act respecting the safety of ships, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

In 1901 an amendment was made to the Act respecting the safety of ships, commonly referred to as the ' Deck Load Act,' and it was found the amending Act of 1901 was so very ambiguous in regard to the height of deck load allowed on open spaces on the upper deck, that it now becomes necessary to further amend the Act to remove the ambiguity and make the law clear on that point.
A deck load law has existed in Great Britain and in Canada since 1873, brought about by an agitation initiated by the late Mr. Plimsoll, a member of the imperial parliament; and up to the enactment of 1901 the legislation in the United Kingdom and in Canada were perfectly in accord.
In the Canadian Act it was provided that after a certain date in the fall no ships could clear from Canada with any cargo whatever on the open spaces in the upper deck to a height exceeding three feet.
It was enacted by imperial legislation that no vessel should arrive at ports on that side up to a certain date in April-15th-with cargo of any description in uncovered spaces on the upper deck to a height exceeding three (3) feet.
The Canadian enactment of 1901 is, however, so ambiguous, that it has been strongly contended that a ship can leave Canada during the prohibited period with a cargo on the open spaces on the upper deck, such as deals, scantling, boards, &c., to a height exceeding three feet, or in other words, to any height which the owner of the ship might consider proper.
The discrepancy between the Canadian enactment of 1901 and the provisions of the Imperial Act was brought by His Majesty's Board of Trade to the attention of His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, and in a despatch from the Right Honourable Mr. Chamberlain to the Governor General, dated the 3rd May, 1902, it is intimated that His Majesty would not be advised to disallow the Canadian Act of 1901, but requesting that the matter be brought to the attention of His Excellency's advisers.
The annexed Bill is therefore framed to obviate this ambiguity and to bring the

Canadian law into accord with the law regulating the loading of deck loads in the United Kingdom.
In the Canadian Act of 1901, paragraph (c) of subsection 1, it was enacted that the loading of ' any deals, battens, or other light wood goods of any description ' was prohibited ' to a height exceeding three feet above the deck in any spaces where the deck of such ship is closed in.' It is contended that this prohibition extends to the cargo only when loaded in covered in spaces, and does not extend to spaces on deck that are uncovered. I may mention that His Majesty's Board of Trade hold this view of the matter.
In the new annexed Bill, which amends the Act of 1901, the limitation contained in those words 'in any spaces where the deck of such ship is closed in,' has been struck out, and leaves the section to read : ' any deals, battens or other light wood goods of any description to a height exceeding three feet above the deck,' that is, above the upper deck.
In paragraph (a) of the same section, the words ' or any pitch, oak or elm planks, or any other heavy wood goods whatever ' are added, as it is considered the addition makes the Act more comprehensive.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speechtext:
It appears to me that this is a very restrictive measure and interferes between the owner of the ship and the insurer. The matter should be left between these parties with no interference whatever. With regard to the height of three feet allowed, I may say that the rail is usually higher than three feet. Why should they not be allowed to have it flush with the rail at least, using that as the measure that would be required? Very often vessels going out from our ports for ports down south load far beyond the rail, and they make their voyages with perfect safety. But this Bill would interfere very materially with shippers from Canada to the ports referred to in the Bill. Is it because it is required on the other side that this should be the case?
The MINISTER OF MARINE Ai\D FISHERIES. Yes ; I read from the memorandum I had before me the recommendation made by the Home government on the matter in order to assimilate the two laws, and have them coincide.

Would it not be well for the hon. minister to remonstrate with the Board of Trade on the other side ? They might allow conditions to be changed to meet the reasonable remark I have made in connection with the load line.

I am afraid they would not find it reasonable, because the matter has been the subject of a very long correspondence, and the Board of Trade on the other side seem to insist that we should pass Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
this law. Up to the present time they have not proceeded against those who infringed the law as it is in Great Britain, but if we do not pass such a law as this, over there.	It	is in the interest	of	ourpeople who	do	not comply with	the	lavover there.	It	is in the interest	of	ourpeople to make this amendment to	the	law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The greater portion of the cargo going to the south would be that on deck. To restrict it to three feet would make it lower than the rail, which, I think, would be a very severe provision. Of course, it would only affect vessels leaving Canadian ports for certain ports on the other side of the Atlantic. But among these shipments are immense quantities of lumber of light material such as pine and spruce, and invariably seasoned, so that the weight would be small. I think it should be left at the height of the rail.

That representation has been made. But' the view taken by the hon. gentleman would not help the question at all. The ambiguity consisted in the fact that the three feet mentioned is inclosed according to the law of 1901. Now, it is proposed to strike out the provision as to its being inclosed and leave the three feet, the same as in the provision of the law enacted in 1901. So, there is no particular change except to make the law clearer on that point.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I only refer to it as a hardship on the shippers.
As I stated to the committee, the matter has been gone into very thoroughly and there is no help for it, if we want to protect our own people.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I remember that when the Bill of 1901 was before the House, there was some discussion as to the meaning of the words ' and during the voyage while'within Canadian jurisdiction.' I do not know whether the hon. gentleman can give us information as to the scope that these words have been held to have since the Act came into force. You will observe, Mr. Chairman, that the Bill says- I leave out the unnecessary words:-
No master .... on a voyage from any port or place in Canada to any port or place in the United Kingdom, or in the continent of Europe north of Cape Finisterre in Spain, not being a port or place within the Mediterranean sea, and during the voyage while within the. Canadian jurisdiction.
*-and so on. What is the scope or meaning of these last words ?

We do not attempt to assert jurisdiction outside Canadian waters. The law is left just as it is, so far as that is concerned-it applies to Canadians in

Canadian waters. If we bad used words having a wider range, they might declare the Act ultra vires. We have no right to legislate so as to assume power outside of our own jurisdiction. The recommendation from the British authorities simply was that the point I have referred to was not made clear, and the object is to make it clear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not know that I would exactly agree with the hon. gentleman's view of the law as to what we can do. But this law apparently means this-that when a master of a vessel gets three miles from shore he can pile up his spars or his deck-load in any way he thinks fit.
But if he does so. he does it at his own risk. He takes the risk of having his cargo confiscated under the law when he reaches the other side.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That would be the case only if he were going to a point in the united Kingdom, but not if he were going to a port, not a Mediterranean port north of Cape Finisterre. The imperial statute would govern the case of a cargo going to the United Kingdom, but in the case of a cargo going to any of these other ports, there may be no law to control it after it leaves Canadian waters.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) ask us to legislate outside of Canadian jurisdiction? I do not think we have the right to do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In respect to Canadian vessels, I think we could.

I have not studied the question, but it would seem to me at first sight that we would not. But I have only taken the law as it stands and amended it to meet the recommendations made on the other side.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

Department o£ the Interior-to pay the claim of Amos Barnes re the purchase of certain buildings on lands situated on river lots, Northwest Territories, $3,580.
['The measure will certainly be announced this week. I am sorry that I cannot give the exact date, except that it will be this week.']

Last year I asked for an appropriation of a similar character, and explained the reasons for it. Some years ago an application was made by Sir William Van Horne to purchase a certain amount of land at Selkirk, near the old town site of east Selkirk, of which he wished to make a model farm. I called for a report from the officers of the department as to whether this land had already been applied for, and the report stated that it was available for sale. Subsequently, however, it turned out that squatters had already settled on the land. There were files in the department to show that these squatters were there and had made claims. I became aware that they were on the land after the land had been sold and patented. The facts of the case are these : In 1883, one John Grant squatted on land adjoining the right of way of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at east Selkirk, and on the 18th of September of the same year he conveyed the same to one Henry Nelson. Mr. Henry Nelson remained in possession until May, 1887, when he conveyed it to Mr. Arnos Barnes, who began erecting a hotel, but before completion of it. in June, 1887, Mr. Barnes sold out to one Frank McRae, who proceeded with the erection and completion of the same at a cost of some $2,500. Mr. McRae having died in January, 1S89, Mr. Barnes leased the place for some time, and in September, 1889. purchased it for the sum of $1,700, and he has been in possession ever since. At the time the hotel and adjacent buildings were erected these were well outside of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's right of way, which was then at this point only 100 feet wide. The Canadian Pacific Railway originally selected station grounds elsewhere, but having decided upon another location, they filed a plan which included Mr. Barnes' hotel, and upon this plan a patent was issued by the department to the railway company, on the 17tli of June, 1895. On this plan, within the limits applied for. I there appears an outline marked ' hotel,'

but nothing to connect it with the claim of Mr. Barnes, who had previously filed a claim for land as a squatter in the vicinity. It was not suspected that the hotel was anything else than the boarding house for the accommodation of the railway hands, and the patent was issued without regard to it. Since that time Mr. Barnes and the Canadian Pacific Railway have had some negotiations with respect to compensation for Barnes' improvements, but no result has been arrived at. In the beginning of January, 1901, the company entered a suit in ejectment to turn Mr. Barnes out of his own hotel, and he then moved those buildings off the railway land on to the other portion of the land occupied by his other buildings, which he had fenced and cultivated as a garden for upwards of fifteen years. At the time of moving these buildings back, Mr. Barnes appears to have been aware of the fact that the land had been patented to Sir William Van Home, but he appears also to have been under the impression that an arrangement had been made with Sir William Van Horne by which Sir William had agreed to convey to the several settlers the lands occupied by them, and it was in consequence of this that he removed from the railway land. The ground on which Mr. Barnes removed his house had been patented, as mentioned before, to Sir William Van Horne, and he in his turn has transferred the same it appears to another party who has instituted ejectment proceedings. This places Mr. Barnes in' a very serious position, and means for him the practical confiscation of his earnings of a life time. This is a case where the officers of the department have made a mistake, I think the department were wrong in issuing patents in the first place. The property has been valued. I asked for a similar vote last year to compensate another squatter, much in the same way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: This represents the value of the buildings erected by Mr. Barnes, does it ?
The valuation was made by a well-known appraiser and valuator, Mr. Wm. Bryden, of Winnipeg, who is employed by an insurance company.
Was it held by the courts that the buildings themselves were the property of the grantee of the lands ?
I do not think the case has come to trial yet. I think it has been allowed to stand at the instance of the solicitors pending action by the government.

The item is simply for the value of the buildings, and it seems to me that Mr. Barnes might have a Hon. Mr SIFTON.
good right to remove them, although he might be ejected from the lands themselves.

I think there will be no doubt that he will have the right to remove the buildings. I do not think there is anything to prevent him removing the buildings if he wants to. I think the parties will be willing to allow him to remove the buildings, but they are old frame buildings, and the real position of the matter is that he has no place to which to remove them. His is a hotel business which he has built up at that particular place, and there is no place in the neighbourhood where he can go. He might as well leave them where they are. I have had this claim before me for two or three years. I did not think at first it was a case in which I should ask parliament to pay it. but after considering the circumstances I thought we ought to pay it. I beg to move :
That the word ' North-west Territories ' be struck out and the word ' Manitoba ' be inserted in lieu thereof.

The reason that I made the observation was that the item purports to be for the purpose of paying for the buildings. It seems to me that you might have a different measure of damages altogether. You are not purporting in this item to pay for the loss of any land. You simply purport to be paying for the loss of the buildings, and I think that very likely he might have a good title to the buildings, and in that event, the department might be called upon to pay only the cost of the removal. If you are not paying damges for the land, it follows that you would not pay for a new site to which to remove the buildings.

I suppose that in reality what he is being paid for is compensation for being disturbed and put out. I finally said, after discussing the thing backward and forward, that I could not put a value on the disturbance of his business and good will, but that I was willing he should get enough to pay for his buildings. The valuation is possibly what it would cost to put up the buildings, allowing a reasonable amount for depreciation. I do not suppose the buildings are actually worth that much money in cash to-day. Rut these are the conclusions of the valuator. In regard to the other ease that we had up last year, we had several parties make a valuation of the property, we had the property valued four or five times, they all differed, and it was a difficult matter to get them to agree. In this case I said : We will have an independent man go out and give us the fair value of the buildings as they are. We did that, and I recommended this to be paid.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any correspondence between the department and Mr. Barnes ?
Yes, I have a recollection that there was a good deal.
Will the hon. minister lay it on the Table ?
There is no objection in the world.
Is there any other claim ? There was one last year and there is one this. Is there any other claim of the same kind ?
I do not think so. There were several made, but these two were the only ones that were well founded.
Supposing a squatter takes up a location on the Canadian Pacific Railway section and is living there and the company sells that laud, has the squatter a superior right to the railway company ?

No ; if a man goes before the land is surveyed and it turns out that he is on an odd-numbered section, or a school section, or a Hudson's Bay section, he has no right to remain unless he pays for the land. , If he is on an even-numbered section, then he has the right to make a homestead entry.
If it is unsurveyed, does he not hold the land ?
He has to take his chances.
Suppose he happens to go upon an odd-numbered section, does he not hold the land ?

No, he has to buy it.

To recoup the government of the North-west Territories, for- expenses connected with the protection of the bridge across the Bow river at Canmore. North-west Territories, $3,000.

That represents the expenditure made upon a bridge in the Banff park by the Northwest territorial government. The bridge was erected by the government of the Northwest Territories just at the time that the limits of the park were enlarged by Act of this parliament, so as to include the locality in which the bridge is. On the 4th November I received a letter from the commissioner of works of the North-west Territories, in which the following statements are made :
I am informed by the engineer in charge of construction. Mr. John Stocks, our superintendent of bridges that owing to the large washouts along the bank of the river in close proximity to the site of the bridge, there is very grave danger of the new bridge being carried away, not owing to any fault in construction,
but owing to the fact that the river is making a new channel for itself practically around one side of the bridge, and that even if the bridge stood, which owing to its construction it is very liable to do. that the channel would leave its present location and render necessary the construction of another bridge practically as large, and that the only method of providing safety is to build protection works for a distance along the bank of the river where 'he wash out has taken place, the estimate of the cost of which is in the neighbourhood of $3,000.
In order to be safe it is necessary to do this work this fall, before the spring freshets get a chance to get in their work.
In view of the actual necessity of doing this work in order to prevent the destruction of the bridge, I was authorized by Order in Council dated December 5, 1902, to enter into arrangements with the government of the North-west Territories to take such steps as might be necessary to protect the new bridge at an expenditure of not more than $3,000. In pursuance of that Order in Council, this vote is to pay them the money.

Amount required to cover the expenditure connected with the opening up of a road from Teulon North, Manitoba, $15,000.

This is to cover an expenditure for cutting a road through the bush country north of Winnipeg in order to enable the swamp lands commissioners and the surveyors to reach the district where they had to work. The expenditure was by error charged to the swamp lands vote, whereas it should have been charged to the Dominion surveys account.
What is the precise location of the road and its length ?
One hundred and eighty miles altogether.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much has been expended ?
It has all been expended.
Was there a vote taken for that work ?

There was not a vote taken for it. The swamp lands commissioners and surveyors went on -to cut these trails in the course of their work, and charged the cost to the swamp lands vote. The swamp lands, how-evef, are, when transferred, the property of the Manitoba government, and when we came to consider the matter, we concluded that the expenditure was not properly charged to that vote, and that the officers Hon. Mr SIFTON.
who carried it on should have applied to the head office for authority. They did not do so, but went on and made the expenditure, considering it part of their work. There is no doubt at all about the utility of the work. I have had it carefully examined by the inspector of surveys, and that is his report upon it. I am perfectly satisfied of the necessity of the work. The error was on the part of the officers in going on with it without advice from the department. If they had applied, I think the expenditure might have been properly charged to the survey vote ; but as the money had been expended, I thought it better to come before parliament and have the explanation made.
Under whose authority was the work carried on ?
The work was done under the direction of Mr. Macdonnell, who was one of the swamp lands commissioners at that time.
Was there a vote taken to cover that service for the swamp land ?
The swamp lands commissioners are paid out of provincial funds, but this item was not properly charged against those funds.
Under whose control are the swamp lands commission ?
Under the control of my department.
Does it not seem extraordinary that they should take on themselves to make an expenditure of that kind unless they had unlimited power ?

I do not approve of the way in which it was done, and, when this came to my attention I said at once that it was done irregularly and could not be charged against the swamp lands account. It was properly chargeable against the survey vote, and under the circumstances I thought that the proper way was to ask for a special vote.
What is the scope of the duties of the swamp lands commissioners V

Under the settlement between the province of Manitoba and the Dominion it was provided that such public lands in Manitoba as should, upon examination, turn out to be swamp lands, to the satisfaction of this government, might be transferred to Manitoba and become its property, and commissioners were appointed for the purpose of making the selection. They report from time to time and their expenses are charged against the subsidy to the province of Manitoba.
I am unable to see what they have to do with constructing roads, if they are appointed merely to determine what are and what are not swamp lands.

The reason given by the commissioner was that it was impossible for him to get on the land to make a selection without making a road. While that is perfectly true, he should have advised the department and asked the department to build the road. Instead of that the commissioners incurred the expenses themselves. I had the matter looked into by the inspector of surveys, and am satisfied that the expenditure was necessary but was not incurred in the proper way.
Was there a demand made on the province of Manitoba to pay this sum ?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was this road inspected before it was built or after ?
It was inspected after it was built and as soon as the question was brought to my attention. The inspector advised me that the road was necessary.

The commissioner who ordered this road, Mr. Macdonnell, I understand, was formerly member for Selkirk V
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

No.
The province will be the gainer ?

No. Of course it will be $15,000 better off than if it had to pay, but it is our duty to do whatever is necessary in connection with the work except pay the actual expenses of the commission. For expenses connected with the Alaska boundary commission (Governor General's warrant), $10,000.

Amount required to cover the late Thomas W. Middleton's shortages in connection with the gold commissioner's office at Dawson, $5,243.14.

This is one of two cases in which there Hon. Mr SIFTON.
have been defalcations, one case in which the money was stolen, and this, a case of shortage. I think we have as good a system as could be devised for the auditing of the revenue in that country. There are a considerable number of offices, in which a large amount is collected. For the purpose of avoiding any possibility of error, I secured, at the beginning, from the Finance Department, the nomination of an officer of the department to be sent there as general comptroller of the revenue. The officer chosen was Mr. Lithgow. I am not sure where he came from, but he has proved a very competent man. It is his duty to see that everything is done that is necessary to protect the revenue. Technically, Mr. Lithgow was responsible for this loss, but, in reality, it occurred when he was out of the country on leave of absence. He reports that this defalcation includes three returns from the Stewart river, those for September, October and November, 1901, some Hootalinquia returns and, in addition the officer took from the suspense account by making false entries. The defalcation was reduced by salary unpaid and other items, leaving it at the amount of this vote, $5,243.14.
What became of this defalcating officer ?

I am informed by my deputy that he committed suicide. There was a change in the office of accountant. Mr. Mackay was appointed accountant and was placed under bonds. Mr. Middleton was appointed assistant accountant. There is where the mistake occurred. When Mr. Lithgow went away the work was divided between Mr. Mackay and the assistant accountant in such a way that the assistant accountant had it in his power to make these defalcations.
I would ask the minister how it was that Mr. Middleton was not under bonds ?

The accountant was under bonds, and he ought to have been doing the work in such a way that the other man would not have power tk) steal this money without his knowing it. If it had been done with his knowledge, the guarantee company would have been liable; but in Mr. Lithgow's absence the method of doing the work was changed in such a way that the assistant accountant got power to handle the money for a short time.
Did Mr. Lithgow make that arrangement before he left about the division of the work 1
I understand from his statements that it was after he left.
Is Mr. McKay responsible for making the new arrangement ?
Mr. McKay would be personally responsible to the government. We would have the right to say to him that he ought not to have made this arrangement.
Did Mr. Lithgow leave any instructions when he went upon Ills holidays ?
I am not quite clear as to that. As I understand from Mr. Lithgow's statement, the change was made after he left.
There ought to be some definite statement from both Mr. McKay and Mr. Lithgow.
If the committee desire, I will have all the correspondence brought down.

The hon. gentleman ought to have it at hand now. It is an important matter that Mr. Lithgow should have neglected his duties in failing to give instructions that were proper, and in allowing this matter to occur. If, on the other hand, Mr. McKay was in authority, and without instructions took that course, then he ought to be held responsible. When was this defalcation first discovered ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
They were both working in the same office, and they did their work in such a way that one mail ought to have watched the other.
I felt myself that in reality, if anybody was to blame, it was Mr. Lithgow.

Has Mr. Lithgow made any statement regarding the matter ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes, he made a full report, which I have here. Mr. McKay did not make any statement.

Has Mr. McKay been called upon to make a statement ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
My recollection is that as soon as the matter came to my notice I at once asked Mr. Lithgow's version of it, as it was pointed out to me by my deputy that Mr. Lithgow was the responsible officer. I placed the blame upon Mr. Lithgow in not having the assistant under bonds.

How long was this going on ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Less than three months.

The report of the commission appointed to inquire into the defalcations in the Militia Department showed rather an extraordinary state of affairs, -and if that permeates all of the other departments, one cannot wonder that there are
defalcations. The report of this commission showed that there was no check on bank transactions and that any subordinate clerk in the office could have committed defalcations without being found out for a year. I hope that such a condition of affairs as that does not exist in the department which the hon. Minister of the Interior administers, because, when there are large sums of money coming in from such a distance, it is very difficult to keep a proper check on them, and unless men are appointed for their ability, and not for their political pull, you cannot avoid defalcations. The wonder is that they are not greater than they are, because the system exposed by the investigation of this commission was utterly bad.

I think the members of the committee will agree with me when I say that in view of the fact that we have officers scattered all over the Yukon Territory collecting vast sums of money, and that we have only lost altogether, out of the millions of money that have been collected, about $7,000, it is greatly to the credit of the officials there. This gentleman is one of the best officers we have, and his politics are those of my hon. friend (Mr. Osier).
That accounts for it.
He is one of the best officers we have, and the government are under a great obligation to him for the conscientious care he has exercised. He made a slip in this case.
You want a larger number of officers of the same stripe.
There is a considerable number.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If they were all Conservatives, there would be no trouble.
There is a considerable number, but I may say we do not give them the preference.

In regard to the observations the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier), if my hon. friend has read the report he is aware that the commissioners did not confine themselves to the Militia Department, but that they investigated the methods of all the departments, and they made a report which was eminently satisfactory. When we think, as the hon. Minister of the Interior very properly says, that only a small sum has gone astray out of the large sums that are received in the Yukon, and when we consider the vast transactions of the Dominion of Canada, we have reason to be proud of our civil service and to rejoice that there lias been very seldom an occasion that anything has gone astray ; and I think that in this respect the members of the committee will agree that the civil service of Canada can

compare favourably with that of any other country- You cannot make a man honest and honourable by any system of examination that you may adopt. At all events, I only wanted to remind my hon. friend that the report of the commissioners appointed to inquire into the Martineau case, and who went through the various departments, was very satisfactory, and although they offered some suggestions, they concluded, as the report showed, that the safeguards and checks prevailing in the various departments were fair and reasonable.

The hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is perfectly aware that it is denied that the report is accurate in some respects in regard to the duties of the Auditor General, and in regard to the manner in which cheques come into his possession. It came under my notice that the Auditor General asked of the hon. Minister of Finance an opportunity of explaining that the commissioners had arrived at some very erroneous conclusions as to the exact circumstances under which cheques passed between the Auditor General's Department and the Department of Militia and Defence.
When the hon. gentleman says that the report is eminently satisfactory, I am not going to raise the question, but I simply think it is due to the Auditor General to say that I am informed that the Auditor General did ask the hon. Minister of Finance for an opportunity of explaining what to him seemed an inaccuracy in the conclusions at which they arrived.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) rather makes out the situation to be much better than I claim it to be, because the report made some reference to the Auditor General's manner of adjusting these things, and the Auditor General complained that the report possibly censured him a little. That does not prove anything wrong in the report, but it proves a difference of opinion between the Auditor General and the commissioners as to what may be the best method of conducting the affairs of the departments. As respects the desire of the Auditor General to make an explanation, I suppose the hon. gentleman refers to the fact that the Auditor General came before the Public Accounts Committee and desired to make an explanation. I offered no objection to his making it, but I suggested that as he was an officer of the House I thought the proper way would be to put his statement in the form of a report, which might be laid on the Table of the House. That is all the difference there was between us in regard to the explanation ; he would like to have made it before the committee, and I suggested that he should make it in a report to the House. I have no objection to him expressing any opinion or making any explanation which he desires to give.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ml-. CLARKE. What change has taken place in the system of audit ?

All cheques are now being sent direct from the bank to the Finance Department, and they pass from the Finance Department to the Auditor General. It has been suggested that they should go also to the department concerned, and that point is under consideration.
When was that change made ?
On the 1st July.
What changes were made in the system of checks and safeguards ?
This change was made as the result of the commissioners' report.
So that the practice which prevailed prior to 1896 continued until the 1st of July ?

There was no change in the methods pursued by the prior government. They were precisely the same as those which prevailed before, but when the report of the commissioners was brought down the beginning of the fiscal year was deemed to be a very convenient time at which to change the system in regard to the handling of cheques.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether cheques are ever signed by stamp by any of the ministers ?
Certainly not to my knowledge.

I ask the question because I notice that very important letters issued by the ministers are signed by stamp, and I think it is a practice that should not be allowed to obtain for one minute. If cheques are signed by stamp i would like to know it. Any one can see what it may lead to. The stamp may be under the control of the deputy or of any clerk, who may be at liberty to sign important letters by stamp. I venture to say that the president, or secretary, or manager of a large financial or business concern, who is signing twenty times the number of letters or cheques that any one of the ministers has to sign, would never think of signing his name by stamp as ministers sign important letters.

So far as my department is concerned, every cheque is signed by my deputy and the accountant in their own proper handwriting. If the deputy is away, the secretary of the department is authorized by Order in Council to sign.
