Is there an Order in Council allowing ministers to sign their letters and cheques by stamp ?

I do not think there is any Order in Council permitting that. There could he no such Order in Council authorizing the signing of cheques by stamps. As to the signing of letters, I suppose that is a matter of the personal taste of the minister. For myself I do not like it, and I have never used a stamp. It involves a little more labour if you have to sign your own letters, but I prefer to sign. I am aware that some of my colleagues use a stamp. I take it for granted that the stamp is only used after they have carefully read the letters. The use of the stamp is a matter of personal taste. As respects cheques I am quite sure they are not signed by stamps.

I am glad to hear that, because judging by the loose manner in which the letters are sent out by the different ministers it is liable to be assumed that they might also sign the cheques by stamp. If that were done no better system could be devised to open the door to fraud and embezzlement.

The practice is simply adopted by some ministers who so sign their names to personal letters. Official documents are never signed by a stamp, although it involves a great deal of labour. Every patent, for instance, is signed by the proper signature of the officer.
I should hope that a patent is not signed by a stamp. I refer to official letters coming from some of the ministers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Some of them are very lazy.

It must have come to the notice of the Minister of Finance especially, that the departmental audit is carried on in a very loose way, and I am afraid that this carelessness is not of recent years either. Any one who examines the departmental accounts before they go to the Auditor General must see evidence of gross neglect. That is especially the case where letters of credit are issued. There is a looseness in connection with the present practice which ought to be put an end to. As the country grows this evil will grow correspondingly. Some accounts came under my notice within the last few days which go to prove that the audit that takes place in the several departments is as a rule a perfect farce.

I think that those who have auy experience with the Auditor General are disposed to bear testimony that whatever faults he may have, he is pretty close in his audit, pretty careful and pretty rigid. So far as accounts which come within his scope are concerned there is very little room for complaint-

I have made no complaint against the Auditor General. I have pointed out that he is utterly hopeless to remedy the evil after the accounts have been paid by the department. There is no more diligent man in Canada than the Auditor Genera L

I was proceeding to say that the Auditor General has not such full control over letters of credit as he has where a particular account is presented to him for approval. Still, in administering the affairs of a large territory, we cannot very well get along without the letter of credit system. If a department has a letter of credit the minister and his officers should realize their responsibility quite as fully as if they were dealing with individual accounts, but unless we abolish the system of letters of credit, I don't quite see how a remedy can be provided. I admit that where a minister obtains a letter of credit the Auditor General loses control over the expenditure until the accounts have been returned, but that is inevitable. If in any particular case a particular minister fails to have an adequate inquiry into the account before paying it, that is a proper matter for investigation and condemnation, but if my hon. friend wishes to abolish the letter of credit system, I would ask him to remember that it would be very difficult to substitute anything in its place in dealing with the business of a large country like this.
I think, Mr. Chairman

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This discussion is out of order.
I do not think so.	%

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is.
It is dealing with the question of the loss of this money and that is a question of audit.

As the Minister of Finance knows, the departmental audit is very often of a very loose character. There are certain cases I think where there has been no letter of credit issued. I do not know that there was a letter of credit issued in connection with the Census Department because that money was not paid until the service had been rendered. I have no hesitation in saying that the census audit was a most scandalous one.
I have no hesitation in saying that the character of the audit by the Auditor General-
I have not referred to the Auditor General.
Who else is it if it is not the Auditor General ?
I refer to the audit in the department before it reaches the Auditor General.

If there is no letter of credit issued, then each individual account goes to the Auditor General and he has the opportunity of auditing it before he issues the cheque. In the case of the census, I assume that there must have been some arrangement under which these accounts were audited in the department and only came to the Auditor General afterwards. If so, each particular account will have to stand on its merits. Speaking generally, I think that the audit of the accounts of the Dominion is in the main very good and very rigid. If we have any fault to find with the Auditor General it is that perhaps we sometimes think that he is a little too rigid in small matters. I believe that the audit in the main is a good one and above criticism, and I say that not for the sake of the Auditor General alone, but for the credit of the Dominion.
No one is attacking the Auditor General.
The hon. gentleman must be attacking some one.
Would the minister state why so large an amount is required in addition to the estimate of last year ?

I would point out that before the spring opened, on account of the apparently large rush of immigration we had to decide what to do. We had to send the parties out early in the season, and we had to incur the responsibility of expending more money than we had appropriated. When we did that, we expected to have the appropriation long before this; but, for reasons with which my hon. friend is as well acquainted as I am, our estimates are late this year. The details of the surveys I gave on a previous occasion.
Whereabouts generally are these extra surveys being made ?

I gave a detailed statement in my explanation of the main vote. It will be found on page 6759 of ' Hansard ' of this session. The greater portion are north of the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, between the western boundary of Manitoba Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
and the foot hills of the Rocky Mountains, in the fertile belt. There are surveys in other parts of the country, but that is where the vast bulk of the work is being done, because that is where the great demand for laud for settlement exists.
Are there any surveys being made of those large tracts of land which are being sold ?

There is a large amount of settlement going on in the land reserved for the Regina, Lonk Lake, and Saskatchewan Railway; and wherever there is a demand for land for settlement, we are carrying on surveys in different parts of that reserve, chiefly in the northern and eastern parts.
What lands are reserved for the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway ?
I could not tell my hon. friend without the map. The land extends from seventy or eighty miles north of Regina to Prince Albert.
That tract has not been extended at all 1

It was slightly extended beyond the original reserve. When the dispute occurred between the trustees for the bondholders of the railway company and the government, the government had then offered to the representatives of the company to allow them to select any odd-numbered sections at the disposal of the government anywhere in the North-west Territories. I sent them a map, and gave them carte blanche to select anywhere in the territories. When the right of the company to the land grant was sold, I did not feel disposed, on account of the changed conditions in the North-west Territories, to allow that offer to remain open, and an order was made, or an Order in Council was passed, confirming their selection to the original reserve, with a few townships on one side, which, if I recollect rightly, included a tract which had been offered to the Saskatchewan and Western Railway Company, but was not accepted. That is the only change that was made.
How many townships ?
I shall have to look that up. I do not remember exactly.
Would the minister give us a map or a description of the lands ?
I shall be very happy to bring down a marked map showing the old grant and the reserve that is passed, so that my hon. friend will have the exact information he wants.
Has the minister dealt with any of the even numbered sections in that district ?

Nothing except the sale that was made to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. With regard to that, the officers were examined before the Committee on Agriculture, and the full details are found in the evidence.

I do not think the evidence given before the Agricultural Committee is printed as yet, so that we are not very familiar with it. Was any portion of the land withdrawn from settlement and sold to this company ? If so, what were the reasons which induced the department to depart from the usual course ?

The arrangement that was made was that we agreed to sell 250,000 acres of land in a certain specified territory at a dollar an acre, on condition that the company placed in each township thirty-two settlers, twenty of whom should be on homesteads, and the other twelve might be on land purchased by them, at their option. I may say that the greater portion of this land was rejected originally by the Qu'Appelle Railway Company as not being fit for settlement, and has been reported by the government inspector as unfit for settlement. The reports of my officers show that any efforts to settle these lands have been a failure. In any case the government would have got nothing in a financial way. The company have not fulfilled the conditions or put themselves in a position as yet to get any land patents.
Within what time were they to put in thirty-two settlers per township ?
They had two years in which to fulfil the condition. The two years are not up yet, but will be in a few months. It is very doubtful if they will be in a condition to get anything.

If the lands are of no value, it is not very probable that they will be settled even by this company. Is it possible, under the law, to withdraw any lands whatever in the Northwest Territories, and sell them in this way to an incorporated company instead of retaining them for the purpose of homestead entries ?
It is.
Will the hon. gentleman give us a reference to the clauses or regulations under which this can be done ? It is a very important feature of the law and we ought to understand it thoroughly.
I will have it looked up in a few minutes.

If it can be done with regard to these lands, it could l>e done with regard to every acre in the North-west. The Minister of the Interior or the Governor in Council could withdraw all the government lands in the Northwest Territories which are still unsettled and sell them to a land company.
The provision is that any particular tract may be withdrawn by Order in Council. Of course, the power is there for the purpose of being exercised in special cases.
It is rather a large power. The hon. gentleman was to have brought down certain papers in this connection.
I found that the motion made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LaRivi&re) included a lot of other things besides this, and I will endeavour to have thp return on the Table to-morrow.

Did Lie hon. gentleman mention the price at which the lands were sold per acre?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
This particular sale was at $1 per acre.

The Order in Council will be brought down and the map showing the tract?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes.

Is there anything in the department to show the value of the land?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.It has all been examined by reason of the fact that it was in a reserve which had been set apart for a land grant to the Qu'-Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, better known as the Regina and Long Lake	Railway. The	railway company
had it examined, and rejected almost all tiie land. It was then examined by the government inspector. He reported that about CO per cent was wholly unfit for settlement. I would have had no idea that the company would succeed in colonizing it had it not been for the suggestion they made that they purposed putting on it a large number of farmers who were accustomed to growing flax on arid ground. For the ordinary farmer it was considered of no use at ail.
'Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). I understand that the company had issued a "prospectus in which these lands were described in very glowing terms?
I am not responsible for the advertisements of land companies.

Possibly, but If the lands are of the character described It would be almost the duty of the department to warn people against being misled by misrepresentations. I have not seen the prospectus myself, but I understand these lands are described in very glowing terms as worth a very considerable amount of money.
They have not put themselves in a position to get an acre yet.
As I understand it, when they have placed thirty-two settlers on a township they are entitled to take out a patent
By townships.
They have not yet settled a sufficient number on any township, so far as the department is aware ?
They did apply some time ago for some of the land, but they failed to put in the necessary proof. They put up .$50,000 as a guarantee that the contract would be carried out.
They have certain rights to get the land at $1 an acre for a length of time. What time are they allowed to comply with the conditions and become entitled to the land ?
When I bring down the Order in Council I will have a memorandum made embodying as much information as possible.
Was there any discrimination made between the even and the odd sections ?
It was a sale of even sections. It was in the reserve. The odd sections they bought from the railawy companies, and they have a right to select what they have purchased from the companies.
The even sections sold were in the territory of the reserve ?
Yes.
Were they between the rivers ? Were they north of Saskatoon ?

I am not familiar enough with the geography to say.
Mr. OSLER, The minister would know whether they were north of Saskatoon and Prince Albert and westward.
I am informed they were all south of Saskatoon.
Have the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company made any selection of lands other than those they purchased from the railway company ? Did the railway company allot their lands before making the sales ?

The position was as follows : The government was under contract to give the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company something less than a million acres of land. A large tract of land had been reserved, out of which the company was entitled to select the odd sections to the extent of about a million acres. The reserve within which they had the right to select was about three and a half million acres in extent. The company caused the greater part of the land to lie examined, and they declared to the government that they could not find a million acres of land fairly tit for settlement within the tract. This was one of the first subjects to come under my attention when I took office in 1896. Protracted negotiations went on between the government and the solicitor for the company, or he may have been solicitor for the bondholders of the railway company who. I believe, had security upon these lands. The solicitor for the bondholders or the company, finally took the position that they could not find within the tract the amount of land fairly fit for settlement that they were entitled to. I then informed them that they might take their land anywhere in the North-west Territories where the government owned the odd sections. I gave them the whole country to select from.
I would like the hon. minister to produce the letter in which the offer was made.

There is no difficulty about that. But the company still refused. There were interviews between myself and the solicitor, when the offer I had made was again discussed verbally. Then, the condition of affairs in the North-west began to change, immigration became more rapid and the demand for land increased. A wet season occurred, and as hon. gentlemen know, this arid land presents a better appearance in a wet than in a dry season. From a combination of causes the land became more desirable. The railway company negotiated a sale to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, the terms of which I do not know.
Was the sale made upon the strength of the hon. minister's letter that they might make a selection in any part of the North-west Territories ?
If so, it was never brought to my attention. The proposition was a proposition from the

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: railway company, and when the sale was made by the railway company, we restricted the purchasers to a certain specified area to which my hon. friend from west Toronto (Mr. Osier) has referred and which will be shown on the map which I shall bring down.

Within the area first indicated ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Restricting the area, not exactly to the original limit, but adding somewhat to it, a few townships.

Then the minister will bring down that map.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes.

How many settlers have been put upon these lands by the Saskatchewan Land Company	.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We have not yet got a return. We must get a return for each township. But they have not proved that they have complied with the conditions in the case of any township yet.

Mr. Turriff, who I believe is a land commissioner, stated, speaking of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company :
I am not prepared to say just how many have Eone in on their grant last summer, but there were over 300 homesteads made in that part.
That was last year. [DOT]

Of course they have sent in a considerable number. I recollect now they applied to get some patents, and they filed some information with regard to settlers. But the evidence which they filed did not prove that they had complied with the conditions, and consequently we did not give them the land.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax. Will there be another opportunity of discussing this matter ?

My deputy informs me there is a small vote for Dominion lands coming down in the supplementaries for 1903-4, which will afford an opportunity of discussing this matter at any length hon. gentlemen may desire. My hon. friend is also aware that he can discuss any resolution on concurrence, with all the information before him.

We are a little handicapped in discussing it at present on account of the absence of the documents which have been referred to. Will the hon. gentleman have any objection to letting this item stand, say, until to-morrow ?

My hon. friend will understand that these are the supplementary estimates for the last year, and it is very embarrassing if 218
we have not got the money available before a certain time. The matter can be discussed just as well and just as fully on other items that will come up.

The minister made a remark that some gentleman on this side of the House knew why the estimates had not been brought down. I hope he does not accuse the opposition in delaying the estimates. I think the opposition have great cause of complaint that the estimates have been so long delayed.

I merely stated the fact, I did not find any fault.
Government of the North-west Territories- additional grant required for schools, clerical assistance, printing, &c., $250,000.

As the leader of the opposition is aware, this is the item that will enable us to pay the deficit of the last six months in the government of the North-west Territories. In the supplementary estimates for the coming year we are going to ask for $250,000 more to add to the subsidy of the Northwest Territories, and I would ask my hon. friend the leader of the opposition to defer the full discussion of the financial state of the North-west Territories until that vote comes up, on account of the absence of some of my hon. friends from the North-west Territories who desire to be present when it takes place. Several of the western members are absent. I will then make a full statement. This $250,000 we desire to pay at once to the North-west government to cover their deficit for the last year. They have expended the full amount of their vote, and we cannot give them any more until this vote is passed. The $250,000 that we are going to ask for will be in addition to the subsidy for the last year.
What is the total amount including this ?
This makes it about $700,000.
The amount last year was $457,000.

I have no objection to pursuing the course the hon. gentleman has suggested so far as making a statement is concerned. I think it important to have the documents we were speaking of this afternoon, printed and in an intelligible shape, and placed before the members of the House before that vote comes up. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was in the House when I drew attention to some documents which have not been brought down in connection with the returns respecting provincial autonomy.

I was away when the motion for the return
ItEVISED EDITION

was passed. I think a large number of these letters refer to financial matters and say nothing about provincial autonomy.

There are perhaps four or five documents which I enumerated in the House to-day which come within this description, but many of them deal for the most part with financial matters, and shortly also with the question of provincial autonomy. It would be well to have the whole situation placed before the House, because the documents will be required in order to enable the House to Judge whether this vote should be passed. They might as well be printed in one pamphlet.
We will have the return made up, including all the correspondence.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to expedite that, because it wrould be important to have it a week or ten days before the vote comes up.
There will be no loss of time. Most of the returns ordered by parliament are prepared now, and we can get a special staff and get this report out in two or three days.

The hon. gentleman does not quite understand me. I said it would be very desirable to have this return in the hands of hon. members a week or ten days before the vote comes up because this correspondence is rather voluminous, and we want time to study the question.
I will undertake to have it down so that the House can order it to be printed this week.

I have no doubt that the particular claim that is being made by the territorial government is a proper one. I am not prepared to question that. I believe the hon. minister is coming to their assistance to relieve them of a deficit that arose from expenditures that were really forced upon them in the interests of the country. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will explain in detail this vote of $250,000.
Briefly, they got a subsidy of $457,000 ; they spent it all, they were $250,000 short at the end of the year, and we propose to give them $250,000 to supply the deficit.
I suppose that they gave the hon. gentleman some details as to how the expenditure was made ?

The correspondence which my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has asked for, and which is very lengthy, goes fully into the financial situation in the North-west Territories, and the different items are covered very fully by it. In order to explain the expenditure I would have practically to read the public accounts of the North-west Territories for the last year. They explain the expenditure of last year as having been urgently necessary,-and as a justification for passing beyond the amount of money that has been voted to the territorial government, they state the fact that there was a very great destruction of their public works by reason of the unusual floods which took place all over the country during the year. The largest item of expenditure, I think equally large with the school expenditure, if not larger, is that which is made on roads and bridges, and the general expenditure on highways, and owing to the excessive floods and the vast amount of damage done they had to incur a great deal of expenditure in repairing the damage. As this was in the nature of urgent expenditure, they felt justified in going on and expending the money. They were the parties responsible for the work and we are not disposed to say that they were wrong and we ask parliament to vote this $250.000. I do not put this forward as a full and detailed explanation, because I will make that in detail when the vote comes down in connection with the supplementary estimates. As the hon. leader of the opposition has been good enough to agree that the full discussion shall be deferred until then. In the meantime I am going to bring down all the correspondence, in which my hon. friend will find the details of the expenditure, and an explanation given of the causes of the shortage and everything necessary to put the House in possession of the fullest information that we have ourselves.

I think they also claim that the immigration going into the country has made it necessary to establish a great many school sections and also that where settlements are made in new districts it has been necessary to provide roads and bridges to a greater extent than existed before. There are a great many items of this kind on which they base their claim." However, we will have a full statement from the hon. minister when he comes to the estimates for the coming year. In the meantime, would the hon. minister l>e good enough to tell us the position of the litigation between one of the municipalities in the North-west Territories and the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to the question of taxation ? If I remember correctly, there were two suits instituted, really on behalf of the government, but nominally by municipalities. One of these municipalities wras in the North-west Territories and another one in the province of Manitoba, and if I remember correctly the decisions in the two cases were somewhat different. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give us a brief statement, because I
know nothing about the matter beyond what I saw iu the newspapers, of what the courts did actually decide, and what is the present position of this litigation.
Does my hon. friend ask me to do that now ?
Just very briefly.

My hon. friend will understand that although the matter arises in a sense in my own department, I do not follow all the details of the litigation as closely as the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick), whose business it is to do so. I understand the present position is this : In the North-west Territories the court held that the tax could be collected on Canadian Pacific Railway lands, and that in the province of Manitoba it was held that it could not be collected. I believe that no notice of appeal has been given by the railway company as yet. I say that subject to correction. As my hon. friend has called attention to it, I will have a proper statement of the exact position of affairs from the Department of Justice, and I will give it later on.
Grant to recoup the local council of the Yukon Territory for expenditure incurred in connection with Eldorado Gusher, $50,000.
If it were anticipated that the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross) would be better here at an early date perhaps it would be better to have this stand.

As my hon. friend suggests that we should allow this to stand until the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross) is here, I would be happy to agree.
# Item allowed to stand.
Military properties-paving streets in front of barracks, Winnipeg, $9,434.
I move to strike that item out. I will put it in the supplementary estimates for the current year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It is no use this year ; the elections are over.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken. It was expected that this item would have been passed some time ago, and that possibly the work could be done before the end of the fiscal year. I intend to put the item in the estimates for the current year.
To pay for land adjoining Hamilton Drill Hall,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
It will be necessary to extend the Hamilton drill hall, and this land was 218}
offered at a very reasonable price and approved of by the colonel of the regiment. I think the hon. member for the city of Hamilton will agree with what I am saying.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I am very glad to be able to confirm what the minister says. There was an opportunity of getting this land very cheap and the price was considered so reasonable that the officers of the regiment got an option to buy it, and it was taken over by the Crown.
Coronation contingent-.further amount required, $13,000.

After the contingent reached London the unfortunate illness of the King occurred, and the contingent returned home about the date it was originally expected it would return. Later on, when the coronation did come off, the King himself expressed a desire that a certain number of men selected from the different colonies should form a body guard, and we sent from Canada a number of 'men commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Turner, V.C. This amount was largely used for that purpose.
To reimburse Lieut.-Col. Cole his costs in Cooke vs. Cole, $1,351.43.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What is this for ?

This item grew out of the suit which took place as the result of an order by Lieutenant Colonel Cole for the arrest of Lieutenant Colonel Cooke, in Montreal, on a charge of insubordination in refusing to obey orders. Lieutenant Colonel Cole was in command at the time of the Montreal district, owing to the absence of the district officer commanding at the Valleyfield riots. I do not know that it is necessary that I should go into all the details, but as a result of this arrest, Colonel Cooke took legal action against Colonel Cole, and obtained a verdict for a small amount of money. A good deal of expenditure was involved, and Lieutenant Colonel Cole lost this amount. In view of the fact that Lieutenant Colonel Cole was discharging his duty, as he believed, as the senior officer in the district at that time, it seemed to me only fair that he should be reimbursed. It is a question of law, which I believe had never before been brought before the courts, and Lieutenant Colonel Cole was acting upon a construction of the law which had been placed upon it for years, and which was placed upon it by the general officer commanding at the time, General O'Grady-Haly. That is the reason this vote is asked.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The minister approved of the course of the officer ?
Yes.
speakername: Tne MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Was there any appeal to the superior officers in connection with it ?
Yes, and the superior officer approved of Lieut-Colonel Cole's action.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: From what I know of the circumstances, it seems only fair that we should reimburse Colonel Cole. How is the sum made up ? Is this the taxed costs, or is there any thing beyond them ?

No. I may say that I submitted the claim of Lieut-Colonel Cole to the Justice Department, and the Deputy Minister of Justice went carefully into the question, and sent me a memorandum fixing the amount at $1,351.43 as the proper amount to pay, being the amount actually disbursed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Should not this case involve some amendment to the law ?

Yes. The Deputy Minister of Justice wns engaged on the matter when he went away, but I am not able to say that he completed it. I had hoped to have the amendment to introduce as a part of the new Militia Bill which I had hoped to bring down this session. That has been postponed, and perhaps the public will not suffer if the two are allowed to go over for another session.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The idea, I suppose, is to place the law in such a position that an officer acting in that way would be justified not only by his superior officer, but by any action in the civil courts that might be taken against him.
Quite so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is this going to be paid to Colonel Cole himself ?

Yes.
Additional unforeseen expenses, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The usual vote for unforeseen expenses is $20,000, at which it has stood for a number of years. But it is really too small, and we have to consider the necessity of enlarging it. The special need of this additional vote arises from the fact that the gratuities to the widows and families of deceased officials are charged to this fund, and there have recently been several large additions to it. There are gratuities to the families of two judges and one lieutenant governor, amounting to a considerable sum. There is also the sum of $692 which was paid for expenses in connection with the visit of the Boer delegates to this country.
Are not these gratuities in some eases brought down in special votes ?

Where they come under the Civil Service, they are included in this vote ; but when there is no provision for them, we take a special vote.
To pay the Canadian Pacific Railway for expenses in connection with the visit of Sir Edmund Barton, Prime Minister of Australia, $1,020.59.

When Sir Edmund Barton was in England last year, he was invited to return by way of Canada, and the government extended to him their hospitality, and they ask this vote to pay his transportation expenses.
To provide for the payment of all services under the Naturalization Act of 1902, according to the schedule of rates established by Order in Council, $6,000.

This is to provide for certain payments which arise under the Naturalization Act, not only as respects the future, but as respects the past, for which returns are to be made, covering a period of years.

I moved some time ago for a copy of these returns. I do not know -whether or not there is any difficulty in bringing them down. I think I had some communication stating that they were somewhat lengthy, but I hope the government will be able to bring them down before the end of the session ?
I remember my hon. friend's request. I will take a note of his suggestion, and will see that the attention of the Secretary of State is called to it.
What is the nature of the returns ? Are they by officers of the courts of the North-west Territories ?
Yes, by the clerks of the courts, and they go back for a number of years.
Are they made to any particular department ?
To the Secretary of State.
What use is to be made of them ? Are they to be tabulated or published ?

I do not know that I can answer that. They are required under the Act. I have no doubt they would be tabulated, but I have no personal knowledge of the matter. They would not be of much value unless they were put in such a shape as to be available for public information.
How is it that they happen to cover a number of years ? Has the work been neglected by the officers in the past ?
I think they are made under a new Act. which is retroactive. Some of them, I think, go as far back as 1853.
Was any vote taken for that service last year ?
No, this is the first vote.
Is the Naturalization Act of 1902 applicable to the whole of Canada in this respect ?
It must be, because the memorandum alludes to some returns which are to be obtained from Montreal as far back as 1853.
From the clerks of the court there ?
Yes.
Does the Act require that we should go back as far as 1853 ?

Apparently. I have not the Act in my hand, but I am reading from the memorandum furnished by the Secretary of State.
To repay Petersen, Tate & Company, the amount of their deposit with interest at three per cent, $56,940.

This
was deposited some years ago by Petersen, Tate & Company as security for their fast line contract; and while we have a legal right to forfeit this money, we think we should repay the deposit with 3 per cent interest. We have no reason to doubt that these gentlemen made every effort possible to carry out their contract, and undoubtedly lost a lot of money. They acted in good faith, and I think the committee will agree that this money should be returned.
There was security by way of deposit and also security by way of bank guarantee. What amount did they cover ?
The bank guarantee was given up some time ago. There were some negotiations respecting a change in the form of contract, and my recollection is that the bank guarantee was then given up.

This represents the end of the bottle neck service too I suppose. If we look back to the debates of 1897 or 1898, we will see that this deposit was pointed to as an indication of the absolute success of the undertaking. We know that in the discussion which then took place, many references were made to this by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We were
referred not only to this deposit of $50,000, but to the bank guarantee ; and when we criticised the action of the government in refusing to carry out the contract made by the government of Sir Charles Tupper, we not only had the pleasure of hearing about this bank guarantee and the deposit of $50,000, but were also taunted with the boast that this government had made a bargain so much more in the interest of the country than that which had been made by its predecessors. I think the difference was said to be a quarter of a million dollars annually. That was paraded, not only in this House, but throughout the country, as an indication of the great business abilities of this government. They were able to make so much a better bargain than the Conservative government, and the service was absolutely assured. There could be no doubt about that. Not only was that boast made in this House, but, on the public platform. In Toronto the rigfit lion, the first minister produced a telegram before a delighted audience, and assured them there was no further question about the fast Atlantic service being an accomplished fact. We asked some questions in the House from time to time, and after a while the treasury benches were not quite so sure, and eventually they got down to telling us that there was no further news on the subject. After a while it was difficult to get any reply at all. Eventually, however, I asked the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce about these two guarantees, and he told us, some three or four years ago that while it was not intended to enforce tile bank guarantee, nevertheless the government did propose to retain this deposit of $50,000, for the present at least. Now this deposit is not only handed back but we are paying interest on it at the rate of 3 per cent. This would perhaps be a good opportunity for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to tell this House something about the prospects of tlie fast Atlantic service at present. This government came into power in 189G with a contract which it could have carried out and which would have been very much more in the interest of the country than any it is able to make at present. From what knowledge I have been able to gather, it would not be possible for the government now to make a contract so advantageous to the country as the one entered into by the Tupper administration. We were told by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, some weeks ago, that it was not the intention of the government to accept either of the tenders which have been put in recently, but that these tenders might serve as a basis for further negotiations, indicating that further negotiations were being carried on. The service which the government called for, and for which tenders were sent in, was rather of an extraordinary character. They called for boats of sixteen knots and boats of twenty-one knots alternately.

The government does not propose to accept any of the tenders put in.' Is there any probability at all that this fast Atlantic service, over which the government has been working industriously but vainly for some seven years, will be realized during the next seven years ?

My recollection of the so-called contract made by the government of Sir Charles Tupper, is that it was one-sided. It bound the government to do certain things and gave the other party the option of doing some things if it suited their convenience. It was not a contract which could be enforced against the contractors. There were privileges and options given them; certain things were contingent on certain other things, so that practically it was not such a contract as my hon. friend describes. As to the deposit, the object of the securities we asked from Petersen, Tate & Company was to give assurance of good faith. No doubt the bargain with them, if it could have been carried out, was an excellent one. It assured us a good service at a much less sum of money than any previous proposition. The fact that it was not ultimately carried out is a cause of regret, but they gave every evidence of good faith. They were a firm of reputable standing, and they furnished, besides this money, a bank guarantee, which was afterwards given up. They gave us every evidence of good faith you could ask of any contractor. They were not able to go ahead, and eventually lost a good deal of money by the transaction.
As to the present position of negotiations I am afraid I can hardly add anything to what my right hon. friend (Sir Richard Cartwright) stated). The government invited tenders for a service of twenty-one knots and sixteen knots. A sixteen knot service in comparison with a twenty-one knot service may seem very moderate; but sixteen knots would be a very substantial improvement on any service the Dominion has ever had. And, if we could get a sixteen knot service fortnightly, combined with a twenty-one knot service fortnightly, we should be in a very excellent position indeed. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce laid the tenders on the Table and stated that they were not regarded as satisfactory, because he thought the sums that were asked for the service were larger than we ought to pay. Practically nothing has happened since. We have not abandoned the question and are still free to receive proposals. Occasionally, gentlemen come to us and say the matter is engaging their attention, and that they will probably submit propositions to us. However, we have nothing to offer the House, and all that we can say is that the matter is still under consideration. We are prepared to make a contract with substantial people. But if they do not come, we can hardly create them. I
do not know what further information we can give.

The government, apparently, is in the position of Mr. Micawber, waiting for something to turn up. I am very glad indeed that the government have not abandoned the question. They have abandoned the bank guarantee, and they are abandoning the deposit. It must be extremely satisfactory to the public that they have not abandoned the question also, but that they still have it under consideration.
Am I to understand that the deposit of $50,000 was remitted ?
That is what we are proposing; that is the purpose of the vote now under consideration.

I agree that, probably under all the circumstances, it is the proper thing to return the deposit; and I think we are getting out of the proposed bargain for these bottle necked ships cheaply. I think we should have been in a bad way if these gentlemen had fulfilled their bargain. The government went into the scheme quite ignorant of what they were contracting for, undertaking a very large expenditure on an experimental ship which has not turned out to be a success for that class of navigation. We are burying one of the attempted bad bargains of the government at very small expense when we return this deposit.

I cannot agree that it was a bad bargain. I respectfully submit that it was nothing of the kind. If carried out it would have been advantageous to the government, in fact, it was so good for the government that the financial men did not find anything in it for them, and they were compelled to give it up.
But if the bargain had been gone on with, as the ships have not proved a commercial success, the service must have been a failure,

I do not think this ship has been proved a failure. Very eminent naval architects have certified that the ships would serve the purpose for which they were designed. The difficulty was not in the class of ships, the difficulty was the financial one. The financial men were not making so much money out of it as they thought they ought to make, and could not go ahead.
Is the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) aware that there are some claims against Mr. Petersen about that deposit ? Are there not some claims filed in the department ?

I have no recollection of them. I must not contradict my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) but I do not remember any.

Mr: LEMIEUX. Mr. Petersen employed | attorneys and refused to pay them and they filed claims. I was asked to warn the hon. minister not to pay Mr. Petersen until these payments were settled.
I will inquire Into it.
I would file a claim for one gentleman
If the claim has not already been filed, I am afraid, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) will find it too late.
I think some were filed.

It is said to be a very bad case that has no redeeming feature, and a very sad case where there is no consolation. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has pointed out that, if we have not the fast Atlantic service, at least we have been saved from making a very bad bargain. It certainly is better to return this deposit than to have made the bargain that gentlemen opposite have proposed. A contract was made by the government of Sir Charles Tupper and was left to be dealt with by the present government. Uut it was rejected solely on the ground that a cheaper service could be had. But hon. gentlemen opposite were grasping at shadows. They endeavoured to make a bargain upon the basis of a scheme that had not been developed, and that no financial concern would look at. The Finance Minister is not candid enough to acknowledge that a great opportunity has been lost to Canada, that it would be impossible to enter upon a contract now such as that made in 1896 which these hon. gentlemen refused to carry out. It is only another addition to the procession of blunders that the present government have been guilty of since they came into office. Now the Finance Minister himself comes down and tells us that the scheme was a visionary one and that financial men would not look at it.
I did not say that.

No, the hon. minister was not candid enough to say that, but that is the substance of his admission. And now he is waiting for somebody to come along and offer him a bargain. These hon. gentlemen evidently thought they had a bargain day arranged' for and rejected the contract of the former government to make another arrangement, no matter what it might be. It was pointed out at the time that their scheme they proposed would be a failure. The scheme arranged for by Sir Charles Tupper's government at a cost of $750,000 to get a cheap service. And now we have
the result-Canada still, after all these years, without a fast Atlantic service.

Will the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) be kind enough to tell me if there was a contract entered into by Sir Charles Tupper's government ? And what was the defect of the scheme which was contracted for by the present government ?
No doubt the Minister of Finance will give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Halifax) his answer.
My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) said there was a contract entered into by Sir Charles Tupper.

I may inform the hon. gentleman from Halifax, if he has not heard of it before, that there was a contract ready for signature, and that this government, when they came into power, tore it up or made some other disposition of it in order to enter into a contract with Messrs. Petersen, Tate & Company, which has resulted as has been stated here /to-night. No doubt the minister will tell him that there was a contract ready for execution on the part of the government of Canada, which contract they did not execute.

I have already stated-I do not know whether the hon. member for Bothwell was in his place ,at the moment-that my recollection of the document, which I have not looked up for some time, was that it was not, in the best sense of the word, a contract at all. It gave the contracting parties an option which practically took away the character of a contract. However, the document will speak for itself.

I understood the member for Bothwell to say there had been a contract signed, and subsequently he explained that it had not been signed by the government. Could the hon. gentleman say why the government did not execute it ?

Iam not in the seertts of the government, and the hon. gentleman has not been kind enough to tell us the reason himself. He is a member of that government, and it is an extraordinary thing for him to ask a member of the opposition the reason why he and his colleagues refused to sign the contract.

I congratulate the hon. gentleman on his ingenuity in evading the question. He knows well that I was alluding to the government which he said had prepared this contract. He said the government of Sir Charles Tupper had secured a contract.

Yes, the ! hon. gentleman said that. He was compar-

mg the contract which he said the former government had secured with the service we were trying to secure ; and in answer to the inquiry of the junior member for Halifax, he said that if the contract was not signed it was there awaiting signature, that is, awaiting the signature of Sir Charles Tupper's government. Now, I understand that document was prepared during the regime of the Tupper government, and was left unsigned by the Tupper government. My question was, why it was left unsigned by the Tupper government.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that matters of that kind may have been going on after the parliament of Canada had expired. These things cannot be done in a day. The question was never raised in the House from that time to this that there was any indisposition on the part of the then government of Canada to enter into the contract that is now spoken of. The hon. gentleman knows that the life of the then existing parliament expired by effluxion of time, and everything ceased at that moment. Those were the ordinary reasons why the document was not signed.

The government to which the hon. gentleman refers as having expired had been in existence, along with its lineal ancestors, for eighteen years. This question did not begin the last month or two of the existence of that gov-* eminent, but it had been discussed for years, and we were told that a contract had been secured that they were anxious to have carried out, and I want to know why they did not sigii it. If it was so good a thing, why did the government of that day not sign the contract 5
And vote the money.

They did not require to vote the money. The member for Botkwell says the parliament had expired, that is true. The hon. gentleman says the contract was made by the Tupifcr government. If, after parliament expired, it is true that the Tupper government had secured the contract, why did they not sign that contract ? That is what we have not yet heard explained to the House.
The hon. gentleman knows that after Sir Charles Tupper went out of office he went to his successors and specially requested them to carry out that contract. That statement was made in this House.
Why did they not do it ?

The hon. gentleman knows that the general elections came on, and while I am not in possession of the reasons, if any reasons existed for the contract not Sir WILLIAM MtTLOCK.
having been signed, it is plain that the question was never raised once inside or outside of this House that there was any doubt in the minds of the government of Canada that the contract should be exs ecuted.
Why did they not execute it ?

Let me ask my hon. friend why they have been dallying for seven years with another scheme ? Will the hon. gentleman tell me now why we have been told year after year that Petersen, Tate & Company have failed ? Why have we been told year after year that the government were negotiating and were likely to execute a contract at some time for a fast Atlantic service ? Why has this been going on from year to year ? I suppose the hon. gentlemen have some very substantial reasons for it ; and yet the hon. gentleman is totally oblivious to any conditions that might obtain during the short period that Sir Charles Tupper was Prime Minister of Canada, why a certain contract was not executed within a few months. The hon. gentleman as minister knows that these things are delayed probably for reasons that might be very valid. Delays will occur, though there may have been no intention of delaying.

I will answer the hon. gentleman's Inquiry why this government has not signed the contract with Petersen & Tate. It is because we have never yet had an opportunity of signing a contract that we deemed satisfactory and in the interest of Canada. When such a contract is presented to us for signature it will undoubtedly be signed. But the hon. gentleman says that they had a contract that was a most excellent one, and that for seven years the government and people of Canada have lost the advantage of a most excellent contract. Now we have reason for it, namely, because the Dominion government, by negligence, omitted to sign that contract.
I did not say that.

If the contract was lying there awaiting signature, and if it was a contract of such infinite advantage to the people of Canada, why did not the Tupper government sign it ? That is a question I want to have answered.

Does the hon. gentleman know now at just what period the negotiations had closed before signing that contract ? Is the hon. gentleman prepared to say that it was not months or even weeks before Sir Charles Tupper went out of office ? There were negotiations upon which that contract was based. Does the hon. gentleman say that there were not negotiations upon which that contract was based occurring within perhaps a week or two of

the time Sir Charles Tupper went out of office. The hon. gentleman is assuming that there were no negotiations for six or seven years, as in his own case. I warn the hon. gentleman that I do not undertake to give any reasons, I am merely pointing out what might be probable reasons. I ask him now if he is prepared to state that he knows that this matter had been a subject of negotiations for any considerable time before the government of Sir Charles Tupper went, out of office, or whether it was a matter that came of negotiations immediately prior to the time of his going out of office.

I presume the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has told us all lie knows upon the subject, just as lion, gentlemen opposite have told the country over and over again that Sir Charles Tupper, after his government was formed, had secured a contract.
When ?

His government was formed on the 26th April, and it lasted for sixty days. Both on the floor of this House and all over the country the hon. gentleman and his party have boasted of his having, during that period, secured a most advantageous contract, and that that contract was executed, but now he tells us that-
The hon. gentleman must not put words in my mouth. I never said it was executed.

Then there was no contract. The hon. gentleman stated in the course of his remarks first of all that there had been a contract secured by the Tupper government. However, he desires, and I accept his explan-nation, to say that there was no signed contract, signed by the government. I presume it was signed by the other party. Was it signed by the other party? If so, why was it not signed by the government of that day ? Why did they not clinch the bargain that was awaiting their signature ? The hon. gentleman asks why we, in parliament, did not do our duty in seeing that it was signed. Sir Charles Tupper had an opportunity of signing it after the dissolution and before we came into office. There was no sitting of parliament while the contract was awaiting the signature of Sir Charles Tupper. Since the hon. gentleman cannot give the information as to why they did not sign it, T think the country will come to the conclusion that it was a very improvident bargain, that it was a one-sided affair, and that the conditions were such as to rob it of its value. I have not seen it for several years-I think a copy was laid on the Table of the House at the time-but I think it was a proposition that no business government would for one moment dream
of accepting. It contained conditions liberating the contractors for all sorts of reasons. The ordinary perils of the sea were nothing to the conditions that were introduced here. They might take their ships off for this reason, for' that reason and the other reason, and the pay was to go on. A great deal of discretion was left entirely in the hands of the contractors. It was not such a contract as the hon. gentleman represents it to be. It was not such a contract as would stand criticism before the House and the country. It was entirely a one-sided contract, and even taking the view that it contemplated a high rate of speed, the details robbed it of its value, and therefore Sir Charles Tupper did not see fit, I presume, in the interests of the country, to sign so unilateral an agreement, and left it unsigned. It was not the contract that the hon. gentleman boasts of, because if it had been, it would not have been left an unexecuted document and used for an electioneering campaign and nothing more.
That is not my recollection of what took place in 1896.

I hear for the first time the hon. Postmaster General criticising the details of the contract. My recollection of it was that the negotiations between the comjjany and the government of Sir Charles Tupper were completed, that everything that his cabinet could do had been done, and that all that was required was the approval of the Governor General. That is my recollection, and I think my recollection is as correct as that of the hon. Postmaster General. It required the approval of the executive, and as soon as Sir Charles Tupper went out of power he wrote to this government urging them to obtain the sole element which was wanting to make a binding contract, because, as far as he was concerned, he had done everything that was in his power.
Wrote to the Premier ?

He wrote to the Premier, and during the late autumn session in 189*), immediately after the election of the 23rd June, Sir Charles Tupper repeatedly called the attention of the government to the matter.
Yes, but previous to that and during the election campaign he stated that the contract was signed.

It was, as far as the government was concerned, perfect, but it required the approval of the Governor Gen-ral. That is my recollection of it. and His Excellency at that time did not see his way clear to give that approbation. As regards the details of the contract, it was

not a one-sided contract, and it was never criticised as a one-sided contract by this government, because it was not. It provided for certain contingencies.
A great many.

The criticism of my bon. friend related to the amount. We were to pay $750,000 and that amount was scouted by my hon. friend himself as an excessive amount, because the government of the day pretended that they eou'd obtain just as good a service, or a better one, for a much smaller amount. That is my recollection of it, and I am quite prepared to admit that we should refund this amount to Petersen, Tate & Co., although I confess I do not think we should refund the interest, I think it would be quite sufficient to return the amount to them, but that is a question of detail. If the hon. Postmaster General says that there was no contract, he must know he was mistaken. There was a contract, and it was completed by the then'government as far as it was in their power to complete it. It was withheld by the head of the executive: Sir Charles Tupper called the attention of the government to the fact that there was this complete and binding contract, but the government never carried it out because they pretended that they could get the service performed for a smaller amount.

I do not know whether it was waiting or whether it was sent to the Governor General for execution or not. If that is the case, and if there was an Order in Council passed and the necessary signatures added, and it only remained for His Excellency's approval, it would, of course, rob my remarks of the force which otherwise would attach to them. My hon. friend's recollection may be quite correct on that point, but when the hon. member for Bothwel! (Mr. Clancy) stated that it was an unsigned contract it naturally occurred to me to ask why it was unsigned.

The hon. gentleman ha< put words into my mouth that I did not utter. I never said anything about a onesided contract, I spoke of a contract. The hon. gentleman became hypercritical, and he wanted to know why it was not signed. I did not say whether it was signed or not.
Yes.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken. It was he who said that, and not myself. The hon. gentleman asked me why it was not signed. I frankly admitted that I knew no reason, and did not attempt to give a reason, but I would like to ask the hon. minister why he at one time opposed the Pacific cable and why he went up to his own constituents and told them that the Pacific cable would bear upon Mr. MONK.
the farmers of Canada, that the Australian farmers would become their competitors in the British markets, that the farmers of Canada would have to bear tbe brunt and burden of the Pacific cable when it was laid, and I would like to know if he has received knighthood for his services in connection with that important work, after telling his own constituents that the burden would have to be borne by the farmers because the Australians would become their confpetitors in the British market ?
Oh, I think the hon. gentleman is imagining a good deal.

If I understand the language of the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy), he said there was a contract, and then he went on to argue that the fault on the part of this government was that they had not carried out the contract. I would like to know whether there was a contract or whether there was not a contract. I would ask my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) to say whether there was a contract or whether there was not a contract. Lawyers, of course, understand what these things are, but it would be better for the intelligence of plain persons if some one would say whether there was a contract or whether there was not a contract.

It is to be regretted that my hon. colleague from Halifax (Mr. Roche) has to pass over the government, wh,o should know something about this matter, and ask for information from the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). However, I do not deny that he is perfectly right in doing so.
Hear, hear.
The Postmaster General has made the rather remarkable statement that the contract with Petersen, Tate & Company never was signed by this government.
Did he say that ?

I understood him to say that distinctly. He said that when the proper contract was brought forward the government would sign it, but up to the present time the government had not signed it. In looking up the records of the debate in ' Hansard,' I find he has entirely different information as to that, from the information announced to the House by his colleague. As far back as the 12th of April, in 1897, Sir Charles Tupper said :
I would like to ask whether the statement published in the newspapers as to Mr. Chamberlain, the colonial minister's declaration on the floor of the House of Commons in England that a contract had been signed by the government of Canada and the contractors for a fast service is well founded.

Yes. Mr. Chamberlain's statement was well founded and the matter is now under the consideration of the imperial authorities.
It was signed, and it was brought down to this House for approval, and parliament passed it, and, therefore, the Postmaster General is not very well informed as to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Yes, I am quite well informed.
My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier said it was the Governor General.

We were talking about the contract between this government and Petersen, Tate & Company, and my hon. colleague from Halifax is talking about something else. Perhaps I ought to apologize to my hon. friend the Postmaster General and say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a misstatement to the House in April, 1897. We will talk to the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he next comes to the House about that misstatement, and ascertain the reasons which induced him to deceive the House in that way. Sir Charles Tupper explained the situation of this contract in April, 1897. In ' Hansard ' for 1897, page 923, he says :
Under these circumstances, negotiations were entered into with the Messrs. Allan and the colonial office, and we arrived at a point which enabled us to agree upon a provisional contract; and all that was necessary, so far as the government of Canada was concerned, was the signature of His Excellency the Governor General. Honourable gentlemen opposite know that an Order in Council was prepared authorizing the government to make the provisional contract with the Messrs. Allan, subject to the approval of the House when it should meet, and so much importance did I attach to this work being carried rapidly and completely to completion, that I took the liberty, when leaving office, of writing a letter to the hon. gentleman who succeeded me, suggesting that if the assent of the Governor General to this provisional contract were obtained, a year would probably be saved. It requires something like two years to construct, with due regard to economy, ships suitable for so great and important a service ; and as soon as the assent of His Excellency was obtained to the proposal, it could be submitted for the approval of Her Majesty's government.
It appears plain that the provisional contract was drawn up between his government and Messrs. Allan. The only thing that was necessary was the assent of the Governor General to the Order in Council, which was not obtained before Sir Charles Tupper's government went out of power. When his government did go out of power, Sir Charles Tupper wrote to the present Prime Minister urging upon him that that provisional contract jshould foe executed; That should leave no doubt in the mind of the committee as to what was the real reason why the contract with the Allans was not carried out. As a matter of fact, it was not carried out by this government
because they distinctly stated to the House that they could make a better contract with (Petersen, Tate & Company. They laughed at Sir Charles Tupper's government because it proposed to give more money for this service than it was necessary, and members of the government of the day whose utterances I have in my hand, threw the taunt across the floor that the government of Sir Charles Tupper were paying altogether too much for this service and that an efficient and equally good service would be provided by this government under the contract with Petersen, Tate & Company at a saving to this country of $250,000 a year. We have had that saving for all these years it is true ; in fact we have had a saving of the whole amount, but in the meantime, we have no fast Atlantic service and according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, there is no immediate prospect that we shall have any fast Atlantic service.

I da not think the country has suffered much by the absence of a fast Atlantic service for thfo last seven years. There are some people who think it is not an advisable service at all. Public opinion is more or less divided on it yet. There are those who favour it; the government would favour a satisfactory service on reasonable terms. But I doubt if any one can point to any injury the country has sustained by reason of not having a service up to the present date. Moreover, it would seem to me- though it is not a considered opinion-that the great development of Canada that has taken place in the last seven years, and the greater development that awaits her in the future, show that the time for securing a satisfactory fast line, so far as the interest of the country is concerned, is rather in the future than it has been in the past.
Why are you advertis-' ing for tenders ?
Trying the feeling ; seeing what we can get.

The Postmaster General has hardly weighed the statement which he made to the House. He endeavoured to cross-examine the hon. member for Both-vvell (Mr. Clancy) and figuring the time he took to do this at $28 a minute, the result has hardly been satisfactory to the House. It is very easy for a distinguished lawyer such as the Postmaster General is to bother and badger an ordinary member of parliament, but I am glad to say that in this instance the hon. gentleman for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) was quite able to hold his own even against this distinguished lawyer and equally distinguished member of the government. The Postmaster General was one of the cabinet who ought to know in what position things were when they came

into power-above all men, at least above all outside of the cabinet, he ought to know exactly in what condition that matter then stood. It does not reflect much credit upon the Postmaster General that lie quibbled for so long a time to-night in order to lead us away from such facts as are important in this connection. The hon. gentleman is always on the alert and in his place in this House if any member of the government is, and he ought to know what takes place, and he must have known of the statement made by Sir Charles Tupper in this House. He knew what was taking place. He knew perfectly well that up to to-night no minister of the Crown had ever dared to say that the question was as to the particular terms of the contract other than the amount of money that was to be paid, under that contract, as proposed by Sir Charles Tupper. But to-night, the hon. Postmaster General Imagining for the moment that perhaps some of us did not recollect the true terms of the contract, and the position in which it was at the time the former ministry went out of power, is so forgetful of his responsibility as a minister of the Crown that he tries to mislead the committee and in that way to mislead the country as to the ti-ue points at issue. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that the question is not a quibble as to whether the contract was signed or not. The particular point is this, that there appeared to be a satisfactory basis of contract arrived at; that Sir Charles Tupper, in going out of office, requested this government to adopt that contract and have it examined and completed in the interests of the country ; that this government professed that they could obtain a contract on better terms and for less money ; that for seven years they have been going through the country proclaiming that they were obtaining a better contract, and leading the people to believe from time to time, that in a few weeks the matter would be concluded ; and that to-day they come down with the statement that they have utterly failed to obtain a contract. The hon. Postmaster General tells us that perhaps after all the country has not lost much ; that he is not sure that, if they had made a contract, it would not have been a loss to the country ; that he is not sure that the bargain which this administration was entering into was not a bad and foolish bargain ; and so he says to the country in the alternative, perhaps we have to congratulate ourselves after all that there has been no contract for a fast Atlantic service. Dees the hon. gentleman forget the speeches he has made in North York, and in other parts of the country in reference to this fast Atlantic service ? Does he forget the speech he made in Toronto at the banquet of the board of trade not very long ago in reference to the vast advantages that were to flow to Canada from the negotiations for transpor-Mr. LENNOX.
tation, the fast Atlantic service included, that were being entered into by this government ? He wants us to understand, tonight that perhaps after all the country is to be congratulated oil the fact that there has been a failure, and that there is no immediate prospects at all events of this government securing a contract. I think the hon. gentleman has hardly done himself justice in expending this long time, at $28 a minute, which he so often refers to, in employing his great skill as an advocate and his great ability as a minister of the Crown, to quibble about a matter which was entirely within his own knowledge, and which, if he did not know it, he should be slow to confess he was ignorant of, having regard for his responsible position as a minister in the administration succeeding the administration which had the contract before it.
Mr. CLaNCY. It would be unfair to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr Roche) to
allow this item to pass without at least recognizing his great thirst for information. The hon. gentleman had the following question on the Order Paper to day :
1.	Did the present government find in 1896, on assuming office, in any of the public departments, a contract signed by the government, or any minister on its behalf, and the Messrs. Allan. f*r, a twenty or twenty-one knot steamship service between Canada and Great Britain, for a subsidy of $750,000 by Canada, and $375,000 by the imperial government, annually. or for any other sum ?
2.	Did the present government find any bona
fide, definite offer to provide the above-named service for the sums .stated above, without any modification or reservation ?	*
3.	What were the reservations, if any, stated in the tender ?
The business government to-day asked that that question be allowed to stand. Is it any wonder that the hon. gentleman should show such undue zeal to-night to ask from this side of the House the very question which the government refused' to answer him to-day ? The committee will no doubt now see why the hon. gentleman's anxiety has been so great. The ministers whom he so religiously supports through thick and thin, were unable or unwilling to answer his question, because they were playing the role of the Postmaster General, a very capable and ingenious gentleman, wlio was filled with information and kept it back for the purpose of a victory. The hon. gentleman has a high position in this House, and it hardly becomes him to talk for victory rather than the truth. That was a small victory, in professing not to believe that the government had all the means of knowing, and questioning those who had no means of knowing, as to the existence of a contract, and basing an argument upon it. I think the hon. Postmaster General lias had a chance to repent, and I hope he has repented. I shall now turn to

the hon. member for Halifax and ask him to press the government for the information that he is asking from this side of the House. It is a most extraordinary thing for a member of the House to ask a question of the government, and the government to request it to stand, and then for the hon. gentleman to ask this side of the House for the information. It is certainly becoming to the methods and understandings of the hon. gentlemen opposite and of this business government, who are always ready to supply not only their own friends, but the country, with information. This is a splendid instance of the business capability of this government, and the plight hon. gentlemen are placed in who are giving them so solid a support.

As my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) has been kind enough to allude to me, I would take the liberty of making a reply. I have heard in the press or elsewhere that the business government which preceded the present one had made a contract with the Allans for a twenty-one or twenty knot service on the most favourable terms, and that this unbusinesslike government had cancelled that contract. My hon. friend from Bothwell alluded to that as a contract, took for granted that it was a contract, argued from it as a contract, and drew his conclusions that that contract had been nullified by this unbusiness like government. I asked the question on that point this afternoon. Either it was a contract, according to my hon. friend from Bothwell, or it was not, according to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I ask these gentlemen, who have a knowledge of the subject, or else they ought not to have talked about it, whether this was or was not a contract ? If it remains to be signed or authenticated by the Governor General or any other power it was not a contract.

I would like to draw the attention of the government to some words spoken by the right hon. the Prime Minister in the debate on this subject. Discussing the Atlantic Fast Line service on May 10, 1898, he said :-
The hon. gentleman referred tio the fact that on a certain occasion I had read a telegram received from the Minister of Finance who was then in England, stating that Mr. Petersen had made a deposit which had been stipulated in the contract. That is so, I read that telegram and the telegram correctly stated that Mr. Petersen had made the required deposit and the money is now in deposit. My hon. friend asks what it is for, if it is simply an ornament. He asks if the deposit has been forfeited. No it has not been forfeited for the reason that it cannot be forfeited. We have no power to forfeit it.

I have not heard yet why the interest should be paid on this deposit. The depositor was given as a guarantee that
the contractors would carry out their contract.. When they have not done that, it seems to me that they should lose the interest on the money. If they get back the principle they ought to be well satisfied.
The general rule with regard to contractors security is that when you return them you return them with the savings bank interest.
Why should they be returned at all ?

That is a matter of opinion. These people have lost a great deal of money. The hon. gentleman says that at least they should suffer the penalty of losing the interest, but they have lost a good deal more. If we do this as an act of grace, we should not spoil it by keeping back the interest.
As the government have lost the interest on this fast Atlantic line these people might reasonably be expected to lose the interest on their deposit.
In this case the government are holding strongly to the principle.

There is every reason to return the interest after the disclosure made to us by the hon. Postmaster General. He has told us that the prosperity of the country and the general trend of trade have led the government and himself to the conclusion that the time was not opportune
I did not say the government.
