That the time was not rife for a fast Atlantic service.
I expressly stated that I was not expressing the opinion of the government. I said speaking for myself.
No, the hon. gentleman may have spoken for himself, but he did not qualify his statement in that way.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I said, speaking for myself.

Well, even so, but when a gentleman occupying the very strong position, the dual position, which my hon. friend occupies in the present administration, takes the House into his confidence and tells us positively that the time is not yet ripe for a fast Atlantic service, we are naturally led to ask him why the government advertised for tenders for such a service. For a long time I have suspected that the cause of 'the delay is to be found in the fact that the hon. gentleman does not believe in a fast Atlantic set-vied for the country at present. Under the circumstances. I am not surprised at; the government returning not only the deposit but the interest. But

we are entitled to know wliy the government, after refusing to carry out the contract made by Sir Charles Tupper, has been continuously holding out to the public the delusion that it was seeking, month after month and year after year, to obtain a fast Atlantic service. We were led to believe that what was preventing the government from giving this country a fast service, was the difficulty of finding somebody capable of complying with the required conditions. But now we have the real reason from the Postmaster General. He tells us that he does not believe in a fast Atlantic service and that it may take some time yet before he himself, if not his government, will come to the conclusion that the time is ripe for carrying into execution the project which has been during the past seven years before this government. Under the circumstances, the frank statement of the hon. gentleman deserves to be taken note of.

My hon. friend is entitled to a great deal of credit for the ingenuity he displayed in twisting words and giving to them a meaning other than what was intended. I have often had occasion to admire the ingenious manner in which my hon. friend has managed to extract from a phrase a meaning different from that which people of common intelligence and sense would give to it. In this particular instance perhaps the hon. gentleman will allow me to recall the substance of what I said. I said, speaking for myself, and not for the government
Well, well, well.
Will the hon. gentleman have patience ?
I cannot have patience with that at all.

What I said was that I doubted if the country had sustained any loss to speak of, because of that fast line not having been already established, and the reason I gave was that the commercial prosperity and growth of the country in the past seven years have been such, that I cannot see how they could have been any greater, and I am confident that in the future more satisfactory results will be obtained than would have been accomplished had we followed the policy advocated by hon. gentlemen opposite.
My hon. friend spoke about the future, and it seems that in his opinion the time for establishing the fast line has not yet come.

We have been years hearing what a great thing this fast Atlantic service was going to be when hon. gentlemen thought they were going to carry through this contract with Petersen, Tate & Company, but now, when that contract amounts to nothing, we have the Postmaster Mr. MONK.
General, after having boasted all over the country of the government's great feats in this matter, saying it was a very good thing that we had not succeeded in the last seven years in establishing that service, and I suppose, applying the argument of the Postmaster General, we must conclude that it would be just as advantageous for us to be without his service another seven years. The hon. gentleman asks us to wait until the country is making no progress, and says that so long as it is being developed commercially, it is not worth while having this fast Atlantic service. The hon. gentleman's remarks throws considerable light on the past seven years. We supposed the government were doing the best they could. We were fully aware that the best they could did not amount to very much, but we did suppose it was the best they could.
Now, it appears, according to the view of my hon. friend the Postmaster General, that it was not the best they could do, that they really believed all the time that it was not very much in the interest of the country that we should have a fast Atlantic service during these six or seven years. This enables us better to appreciate the position of the government with regard to this matter ; and the House and the country ought to be very much obliged to the Postmaster General for the frankness with which he lias expressed his opinion with regard to the very important subject.

If the explanation had not been given, I certainly would have left this House with the idea that the government were satisfied that the negotiations for the fast Atlantic service had failed. The Postmaster General, with his important position in the cabinet, must have great weight, he has expressed so freely the opinion that it is as well for the country that the fast line negotiations have failed, that I think it would be well for us to know where he is going to stand on this question, for it is a very important question, and one that will involve a very large expenditure if it is to be gone on with. And I think we should know whether his colleagues agree with him on that point, for I believe the country regard it as a very important matter. And I am much mistaken if there will not be a great feeling of disappointment in the country when it is found that this government, instead of being in earnest on the question of a fast Atlantic line, have all the time been playing false, have all the time been fooling the country. I remember being present at a banquet in Toronto, and I think the Postmaster General was there also. A cable came, timed to the moment, just when the Prime Minister was speaking. It was from the Minister of Finance, then in England, and stated that the contract had been concluded for the fast Atlantic service, the deposit secured and everything completed.
[ If I mistake not, the Postmaster General was among those who applauded
No, I was not there, nor did I applaud.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. However, I believe that that applause represented the feeling of tlie country-that there was general delight that the fast Atlantic service had been secured. I think the discussion we have had to-night shows that, to all intents and purposes a contract had been	made with the
Allans which would have given to this country a fast Atlantic service, and that this government, when they came Into power, threw the contract aside. I was in the House during the discussion on the reasons for throwing it aside, and my. recollection is that the only reason given-at all events, the only reason that had any weight-was the extravagance of the contract. I do not think it is well now to try to get out of the responsibility for *cancelling that contract by pleading a mere side issue in the conditions, particularly as the government made no attempt to renew the negotiations with Messrs. Allan, but at once set about making a new contract with *other people on the plea of economy. The contract with Mr. Petersen failed, as all men who had experience with mercantile business knew it would fail, for it was not entered into on a business basis, but purely on an experimental basis. I say this government had no business to enter into a contract of an experimental nature on. such a subject. The Petersen contract having failed, and the deposit being the only thing that keeps in mind this great failure, I throughly agree to the return of that deposit. and I agree with the minister in thinking that if the deposit is paid back, interest at 3 per cent should be paid. And I shall be glad to see the end of the Petersen contract.

I sup-Xiose that gentlemen who attend great banquets In Toronto where the proceedings are marked with great enthusiasm should not be held too closely to their recollection of what occurred. I suppose, we shall have to forgive my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) if he depends upon a naturally fertile imagination, cultivated under very pleasant circumstances, in reporting statements coming by cable from the Minister of Finance, rather than upon any record of the facts. The hon. gentleman says that a cable was handed in, timed to the moment, stating that the contract had been concluded, the deposit had been made and all sorts of arrangements completed. The only foundation for the statement was that a telegram was read on that occasion from the Minister of Finance, not stating that the contract had been concluded, for it had been concluded months before, not stating that all arrangements had been made, but simply that the deposit had been made. That was the fact. The deposit had
been made. The cablegram stated the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

But on the basis of the telegram, speaking from memory, all that I have stated was set forth. It was stated that this telegram marked the conclusion of these negotiations, that practically the transaction was completed, and the fast Atlantic service secured. I have been quite within the mark and have been speaking without exaggeration in the statements I have made.
But my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) stated that all these things were set forth in the telegram from the Minister of Finance.
That was a mere detail.
What difference does it make ?
Well, when anything is quoted as having come from me, I like to be correctly quoted.

I do not think I misrepresented my hon. friend the Postmaster General in the view he took of the fast Atlantic service 1 He has admitted that the past attempts to secure that service have been fruitless. I think he went further, and stated that the country at the present moment did not require that service.
I did not make any such statement.
That will be borne out by ' Hansard.'
Not at all.

I think that as this is essentially a government of individual opinion. We are entitled to know the opinion of the hon. gentleman's colleagues. We have here the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), who is interested in the fast service. The Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine). I think that, under the circumstances, we are entitled to an individual expression of opinion from these gentlemen as to whether they coincide in the rather scornful expression of opinion we have heard from the Postmaster General as to this very important matter.

I am very glad to say that I can now furnish the Postmaster General with the information he pressed so strongly for. He wanted to know why the contract, if any, had not been executed. I frankly admitted that I was not prepared to offer any reasons.
Why, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) gave several reasons.

That is the hon. gentleman's (Hon. Sir William Mulock) language, not mine. The hon. gentleman pressed me very hard, because he wished the committee to believe that there was some substantial reason why that contract, if not executed, was delayed. That was the hon. gentleman's object, if he had any. There was no other object apparent from the course the hon. gentleman took. The reasons I gave were that posibly there was not time. Now I am going to read from a return that was brought down in connection with the fast Atlantic service. Here is what Mr. W. G. Parmalee, deputy minister, has to say :
Sealed tenders addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, care of the High Commissioner in London or to the undersigned, marked on the outside ' Tenders for steamship service, Canada and Great Britain,' will be received at the office of the High Commissioner in London, or at the Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, Canada, up to and including Wednesday, June 10th, 1896.
That was the first time tenders had been asked for, and these tenders were to be received up to and including 10th June, 1896. AVe have a report here from the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, the late hon. W. B. Ives, dated 30th of June, 1890, of which I will read the first paragraph :
The undersigned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has the honour to submit for the consideration of His Excellency the Governor General in Council the following :
Under the authority of an Order in Council of date the 6th of May, an advertisement was inserted in various Canadian and English papers asking for tenders for a ' fast Atlantic service,' under certain terms and conditions, copies of which, as hereto attached, were distributed to various steamship companies and to parties asking for the same. There were, within the time specified, three documents handed in at the office of the High Commissioner in London, endorsed ' tenders for steamship service, Canada and Great Britain,' and one was handed in at the Department of Trade and Commerce. I
I shall not read further than that. It is evident that the reasons I gave, while not the real reasons, were perfectly true and obvious, namely, that possibly there was not time. The hon. gentlemen will see from what I have read that in the first place tenders were asked for on the 6th of May, 1896, and the last day for receiving such tenders (was the 10th June, 1896. The elections took place on the 23rd of June, and this report made on the 30th of June by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, set forth that these tenders had been asked for, and asked practically the assent of the Governor General in Council to the contract, and the government resigned on the 11th of July following. Now,
I would ask the hon. gentleman, in face of the return that has been brought down, and of which I have made a slight quota-Sir WILLIAM MULOCK-.
tion, if it was not a fair suggestion to say that possibly there was not time to execute the contract.

I agree with the hon. gentleman In his last statement that when tenders were only received on the 10th of June, it was not unreasonable that the government should not have signed the contract on the 30th of June. I should be surprised if a contract of that magnitude could be dealt with in twenty days. The hon. gentleman has thrown some light on the subject by giving dates. But at the same time he does not dispose of the question. His party had been 18 years in office, and had had ample time to formulate a policy and carry it into effect if they desired. Why did they delay signing the contract until after they were defeated ?
I would ask if the penalties attached to this contract with Petersen & Tate were ever called for by the government ?

I do not recollect what penalties there were other than the deposit of the security in cash and the bank guarantee. The bank guarantee was given up several years ago in connection with the readjustment of the contract.
What is the date of the Toronto meeting ?
6th of October.
That is not the same time, nor anywhere near it.
This agreement was made on the 22nd of March, 1897.
That is farther away yet from the October telegram.
This was on the 22nd of March in the spring and the meeting in Toronto was in October.
My hon. friend said that it was about the time of the Toronto meeting and he finds it was far away. *

It was near enough to suit the purpose of the right hon. Prime Minister in reading such a telegram with the object of influencing the electors. There is no question about the penalties attached. If the company did not build their vessels after a certain time, if they did not do certain things at a certain time there are penalties mentioned in this contract.
Yes, the deposit and the guarantee. These are the penalties.

Yes, but in addition to that here is one of them :
Subject to the conditions hereinafter contained.. there shall be paid to Her Majesty as liquidated damages agreed to by the contractors :-
(a.) The sum of five hundred pounds on each occasion when the contractors fail to provide at the appointed Canadian or British port a mail ship in accordance with contract, ready to put to sea at the appointed time, or when such mail ship shall not actually put to sea and proceed on her voyage at the appointed time.
They would be very poor If we enforced that.

Why is it that these contractors were to be allowed 3i per cent and the hon. gentleman is now only allowing them 3 per cent. I think the government should not allow them any interest at all. I think they are doing very well to get their $50,000 back and this government have been lax in the performance of their duty in not demanding the payment of the forfeit by this company for failing to enter into this contract. It is well known that prior to 1890 one of the strongest supporters in the fast Atlantic service was Sir Charles Tupper. He came to this country in 1896, he became the premier of Canada, he acted in that capacity for sixty days and during that short period of time, as is conclusively shown by the Blue-book, the government of which he was the head were fully alive to this important question. As the result of advertisements asking for tenders to be closed on the 10th June, they had a contract prepared, signed by the government, and agaiting the signature of the Governor General. So, I say it does not lie in the 219
mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite to charge the government of that day with laxity in their duty to try and bring about this fast Atlantic service. But, this is in line with the policy of the Liberal party since 1890. They have no policy upon any particular question. They are simply opportunists. Even after they have' agreed on measures in Council and before bringing them down to this House, if popular opinion is against them they are prepared to revoke their measure and come down with a different policy next day to meet public clamour. When the government of the Conservative party ruled this country and when the hon. gentlemen then occupying seats on the opposite side of the House asked the government of the day where they stood on any particular question, the Conservative leader of the government rose up and declared their policy. If the opposition of that day asked any question concerning the policy of the government in any particular line the Conservative party were ready to state their policy.
They were great on policy.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon ?
They were better on policy than performance.

They were a constructive party while hon. gentlemen opposite are a destructive party. That is the difference between the two parties. The Conservative party in opposition are not afraid to declare their policy. They are prepared to declare their policy on any line in regard to the government of this country, while the government lucks stamina and backbone enough to state what they think upon any question, and especially what their policy is in respect to the railway question. People have come to the conclusion, especially since what transpired here the other day, that the government are not prepared to announce themselves on any important or serious question. In addition to what I have said I desire to add that I think it is a crying shame that the business of the session should be in the position we find it to-day. When the speech from the Throne was brought down over four months ago, I want to know if the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurler) had it in view then to keep this House in session and to keep this opposition waiting for over four months for its policy to be presented on the transportation question. Did he have that in view at the time he came down with the declaration which was put in the mouth of the Governor General ? If he did not have that in view, how does it come that we have been kept here for four and a half months and that the government are not prepared to state to the opposition and to the country what their policy is upon the transportation ques1



tion ? It is a crying shame and I want to repudiate the assertion that is often made by hon. gentlemen on the other side of * the House that the opposition are to be charged with obstructing the business of the House. We are adopting the only legal and proper course that is open to the opposition, namely, to call the government to account for having failed to bring down important legislation that was promised to this House months ago. When the right hon. Prime Minister said the other day that it required courage and boldness to introduce a question of that kind a broad smile spread over the countenances of members of the opposition because we did not expect from the leader of a great party that it required boldness or stamina to come down and proclaim his policy.
We are getting a little out of the track of the fast Atlantic line ?
It is a little out of the track, but I think it is a good thing to remind hon. gentlemen of their shortcomings.
Is it not congenial ?
Oh, very.

The sooner hon. gentlemen proclaim their great measures which they propose to bring down to this House the sooner we will get through. In the meantime, as a humble member of this House, I want to deny that any hon. member on the opposite side of the House has any right to accuse any hon. gentlemen on this side with obstructing legislation?

To show that I did not exaggerate in the statement I made as to the effect of the celebrated cable, in regard to which, as the hon. Minister of Finance said, I was quoting from memory, I shall quote the ' Globe ' report of the banquet, which will show how" genuinely in earnest apparently the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues were at that time. This is from the ' Globe ' of the 7th October, 1897, and the banquet was on the 6th October :
If I find anything good in the programme of my predecessors-I hope Sir Frank Smith will not accuse me of any theft if 1 say so-(laughter). I am quite willing to put on the clothes of Sir Frank Smith, and they would be a good fit. I am sure. (Laughter). The government of which Sir Frank Smith was an honoured member had determined to have the fast Atlantic service, that is to say, the service to carry passengers especially, and to carry the mails. But, you know. I must say, though it be in the presence of Sir Frank Smith, that we are above all things an economical government. (Laughter).
What roars of laughter there would be if the right hon. Prime Minister had said that at a banquet at the present time !

That is a compliment which I cannot pay to the government of which Sir Frank Smith was a member. (Laughter). I wish I could ; but the truth, you know, must be the truth upon all occasions. (Laughter). Sir Frank Smith's government had undertaken to give to that service a bonus, a subsidy, of $750,000 a year. We thought it was too much. We thought we could do it for less, and we succeeded in making a contract with a firm for a subsidy of $500,000, saving to the country therefore the sum of $250,000. We contracted with the firm of Petersen Tate & Co., a Newcastle firm, a firm composed as we ascertained, of men of the highest honour, of the highest integrity, and the highest competency in their profession. Mr. Petersen and Mr. Tate have had a good many obstacles to overcome, [DOT] as is always the case with men who launch a new idea into the world.
Here the Prime Minister acknowledges the truth of what I said, that it was a new idea and an experiment, and It turned out to be a fad.
Their idea was a new one, and therefore it met with objections and with discouragement from more than one class of people ; and not later than a few weeks ago, or a few days ago only, it was stated that the scheme of Mr. Petersen had fallen down, that it must be considered as absolutely a thing of the past. Mr. Petersen and Mr. Tate were at work. They work as men always work when they want to succeed. They said nothing ; they answered no accusations ; but to-day I have a telegram from my friend and colleague, Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance, to this effect : ' Petersen has made to-day the deposit required by the contract.' (Loud cheering and great enthusiasm).
The contract was signed and the deposit was paid. I was quite mild when I quoted the enthusiastic manner in which the Prime Minister elaborated on this.

It was the enthusiastic manner in which the telegram was worded.
Mr. OSLER, Well, I was quite right anyway.
It is with joy indeed that I welcome this explosion of satisfaction at the announcement that this scheme has not failed, but that it is to be carried through. I know that in some quarters this idea of having this passenger traffic amongst us was not popular ; but, sir, let me say to you that if there is a patriotic idea in the land it is the idea that we should not only carry the freight, but carry the' passengers between America and Europe. (Hear, hear, and applause). We can do it, we ought to do it, and now it is no longer in doubt.
What will the Prime Minister say to the Postmaster General's doubting to-night.
This line of steamers shall be floated probably within two years, certainly within three years ; and when we have this class of steamers afloat on the ocean I have no hesitation in saying, such is my confidence in the scheme-and it is a confidence which must be borne by every man who has looked into the subject-that we shall have the great bulk not only of Canadian traffic, but of American traffic as well, Sir, remember this, what I say is no idle boasting. Remember that the St. Lawrence route is the shortest of all routes. Now, as you know, all | men have an aversion to the sea-I know I have

-(laughter)-and my experience is not txcep-tional in this respect ; all men have a terror of the sea ; but when tourists know and are aware that upon the Canadian line, with a class of steamers having a speed of twenty knot3 an hour, equal in comfort to the best afloat on the ocean, there will be no more than four days between land and land-(applause)- the Canadian line will be patronized as no other. (Great cheering). What will be the case when this line is in operation ? The case will be this : that a passenger taking the steamer at Moville. say, if Moville is to be the Irish port, within less than four days will be in the strait of Belle Isle, and then within less than one day, or twenty-four hours, will be in the harbour of Quebec, and one day's sailing on the beautiful St. Lawrence with its magic scenery and free from all discomforts of the sea. (Applause). When we have this line with us we shall not only have the entire Canadian traffic, but we must as a necessity have the larger proportions of the American traffic. This that I say may perhaps seem presumptuous. It is not. At all events, if it is, I have such an unbounded faith in my ceuntry that I believe every word that I say now and I am sure it will come (.ut to be true also.
I do not think I can be accused of having exaggerated.
Who made that speech.
Why, that was the Prime Minister before an audience in Toronto.
Oh.
When.
In October, 1897.
Oh.

I think I was quite right: when I suggested that the cablegram was in beautiful time. I have no doubt it had been waiting in the office for a considerable time and it was brought out and its date altered so as to make it opportune, and it was received with tremendous applause. It was the key note of the meeting; that the government had succeeded in securing a fast Atlantic service equal to the best on the continent; that they had repudiated the contract that had been made .with the Allans; that as an economic government should, they would save the country $250,000 a year, and that in two or three years at the outside the most magnificent fleet of boats on the ocean would be sailing from Quebec to Europe. This was a very poetic vision, but when it came to fulfilment the government were entirely unable to get any futlier than the initiatory stage, and the Minister of Finance had the deposit and he has held it at a rather high rate of interest for the benefit of the country ever since.
The hour is late but I beg to rise to say that I am troubled about the speech of the Postmaster General. I feel a great deal of anxiety for him. He says he has been speaking for himself.

Oh, oh.
219*
He will be out tomorrow.
He is the master of the administration now.
I think that the rule has been laid down very clearly that a Minister of the Crown in this country of ours has no right to speak for himself.
Hear, hear.

In England they have such a right, but England is a small country and the constitutional rule is not well known nor well understood. In Canada a Minister of the Crown has no right to speak for himself. Now, the Postmaster General has either spoken for himself or he has spoken of somebody else. If he has spoken for himself he has violated the constitution.
Hear, hear.
I am very much afraid that he will be punished and his punishment will be severe indeed if he is punished as he deserves to be punished.
Hear, hear.

If the Postmaster General has spoken for the government he has no right to say that he was speaking for himself. We are in a difficult position. We have the right to know, when a minister of the Crown speaks in parliament, whether he speaks for the government or whether he speaks for nobody at all.
Hear, hear.

He has no right to speak for himself and if he does not speak for his colleagues he speaks for nobody. I am anxious to know where we stand tonight. We have heard a great deal about the fast line. The Postmaster General has reproached one of our friends with the statement that he was off the track. I would like to see the track of that fast line.
Hear, hear.

If there is any track to that fast line at all I want to know where that track is.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) To Halifax.

In the winter months Halifax is the right track, but I would like to know what track the government intends to take in the summer months. One member of the government said that it was premature to expect that the contract should be awarded now. I have some experience in awarding contracts and, when tenders are asked it is an evidence that the plans are matured and that the tenders are to be decided upon. When those tenders were asked the government had a policy and the country has a right to know when the government will adjudicate upon the tenders.

Parliament is sitting and in my liumlile judgment I think it is the proper time to decide upon this very important matter. We have been years and years trying to arrange for the fast line. I am not prepared to say that the government have not done the best they could, but that best has not been much. I am very sorry to say so, but perhaps it is just as well that we have not decided sooner. However, it seems to me that now that the government have asked for tenders, and having told the country that they were ready for the question, they should take the House into their confidence and decide one way or the other. Rut. again. I am very much afraid my hon. friend the Postmaster General is swimming in deep water.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I must pay my hon. friend the courtesy of recognizing his remarks ; I quite understand the tenor in which they are expressed. He is quite aware of the efforts made by the government to secure the fast line ; it is all a question of terms. It' the people of New York desired a line, they could have one, as that city affords such attractions on very satisfactory terms. Our own Canadian ports are coming to the front, and becoming more and more attractive to shipping, and as the days go by, we shall be able to make better terms. The government, ever since it was formed, has been prepared to enter into a contract if satisfactory terms could be secured; and I think, with the progress the country has made, is making, and is sure to make, that a satisfactory contract may be looked for in the near future. It is, however, a question dependent on the amount the country is prepared to pay, and the cost in turn depends on the attractiveness of the route itself. If Canada were a sufficiently populous and wealthy country, we would not have to pay a subsidy; we would have fast lines coming here because it paid them to come. But all things go by comparison. My hon. friend is quite aware that we are as anxious as the opposition to have a fast line when it can be obtained on terms which will be deemed to be satisfactory.

I think it is a fortunate thing that no contract has been entered into, and I am surprised to hear hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House speaking of this as a fast line. It is no such thing ; it is a slow line. With the progress which Canada is making, and with the intelligence of the people, I think we must one of these days have a fast line that will be worthy of the name. Of course, the selection of the route is a question for the future to decide ; but when we find ourselves so many knots below what is the case elsewhere, we are very far behind the times if we speak of this as a fast line. I am well pleased that no contract

has been entered into, because we would be only the laughing stock of other nations if we dared to call what Canada has a fast line.
Amount required to meet the expenses of the royal commission appointed to make inquiry into recent industrial disputes in the province of British Columbia (Including payments not exceeding $5 each per day to members of the civil service for services in connection with this commission, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act), $10,000.
What is the position of the work of that commission at the present time ?

This commission was appointed this spring to make an inquiry into the clauses of the industrial disturbances in the province of British Columbia, which have been more or less frequent for some time. This spring there were strikes in the city of Vancouver, and at the Union and Extension coal mines. The inquiry was conducted by two gentlemen, Chief Justice Hunter and Mr. Elliott Rowe.
What is Mr. Rowe's occupation or profession
Are all the strikes over in British Columbia now ?

I think that is the ease. The strikes at the coal mines and on the railway are settled now. Calgary is not in British Columbia, but there was a carpenters' strike there which paralyzed many other industries. That strike, which had been in existence for many months, has now been declared off. These men have resumed work and requested the deputy to arrange for a standing agreement between the men and their masters for the settlement of the future disputes so as to avoid strikes. My deputy informs me that the employers have agreed to that arrangement and have even gone further. They have entered into its spirit and since the men have consented that there shall be no strike without an appeal being made first to arbitration, they, in a like manner, bind themselves not to lock out without first referring the dispute equally to the standing board of arbitrators for Calgary. The coal mine strikes at Union and Extension mines had been in existence for several months and was due to causes which will be made quite clear when the report is presented to parliament.
How many days was this commission sitting altogether ?

The commission issued towards the end of April and lasted continuously. I fixed a date within which the work was to be completed so that there might be no delay. The deputy told me that the report of the commission alone covers about 150 pages of type written foolscap and that the evidence is most voluminous. It was taken in public meeting, the court-house being thronged, and the questions fought out well on both sides by counsel.
Who were the counsel ?

There may have been different counsel at different places, but, I recollect the names of some that my deputy gave me. One of the counsels was Mr. Wilson, a member of the British Columbia government, another was Mr. E. P. Davis, a leading counsel in the city of Vancouver. There may have been others whose names I have not heard. I think flint Messrs. Wilson and Davis were representing the employees. Mr. Bodwell may have been engaged in the case as well, but that I do not know.
I notice that this item is for $10,000. Were there any other charges?
None whatever. This is the total amount.
What pay do the commissioners receive ?

There were two members of the civil service on that commission. One was Mr. King the Deputy Minister of Labour, and the other a short hand writer in the Labour Department. The item of $5 per day each is for those two.
Were they getting this over and above their own salary ?

Yes, and it was very reasonable that they should have it. It is quite impossible for people travelling to make up 'for themselves their legitimate disbursements. There are many small items of disbursement, which are not strictly taxable in their living expenses, but which they have to pay.
Their expenses were paid, apart from this $5.
The $5 was to cover any expenses over and above living expenses.
What was the pay of the commissioners per day ?
I think the Chief Justice was paid $40 per day. I do not remember what the others were paid. There will be some printing to pay for too.
Did the hon. gentleman not pay a substitute for Rev. Mr. Rowe ? While he was away, who looked after the spiritual wants of liis people ?
I do not know that he has any charge.
What demand was there for the appointment of this commission ?
What does the hon. gentleman mean ?

I remember the hon. gentleman making the statement that the Labour Department were now ready to cope with strikes in the different parts of the country. He instanced Vnlleyfield, and sent his deputy to Rossland to look after a gold strike. I would like to know whether the hon. gen-
Will the hon. gentleman give us the information later ?

Yes; of course these items will appear in the Auditor General's Report.

698S
tleman has found his department unable to cope with these strikes, and for that reason has appointed a commission.

The object of this commission was to take evidence. It was a semi-judicial tribunal, clothed with the power to take evidence and examine witnesses under oath. The chief justice is eminently qualified to weigh evidence and draw conclusions. That commission has rendered great public service. I have already heard from British Columbia satisfactory expressions of opinion as to the good it has accomplished, and my hon. friend will put himself and his friend in a false position in the eyes of the people of that province, if he should assume an attitude of hostility to that commission. The commissioners were men of eminent standing and knowledge and had the confidence of both parties. It has restored harmony and brought to light circumstances which were hidden and will be most interesting and valuable to the industrial world.

Two or three years ago serious difficulty arose in the mining districts in British Columbia. The hon. minister sent his deputy out there for the purpose of bringing about a settlement; and I think that both sides were dissatisfied with his ruling. I suppose the state of feeling was such there that those who had invested capital and those employed in the mines thought it was as well a commission should sit for the purpose of inquiring and placing the facts before-the House, so that members could find out where the cause of the trouble lay. I presume that the hon, gentleman from the North-west Territories who introduced the Bill in another portion of this legislature for the purpose of preventing foreigners coming into this country to agitate strikes was largely prompted by the difficulties that occurred in British Columbia. If we have the information that this commission have to-day, it may be useful for us, and if the hon. minister will lay it before the House before some of the Bills now coming up for consideration are passed, it may assist in the discussion of those Bills.

I requested the deputy to-day to have the report printed with all despatch, and I have no doubt he already has placed it in the hands of the printer. He only arrived to-day. My hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) is entirely misinformed as to the supposed state of feeling in Rossland and of the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Labour. The Deputy Minister of Labour was invited to Rossland to deal with troubles between employers and employees in the mining districts. There was a strike-
A couple of years ago.
Not so long ago as that, I should think. He -went

there and investigated the cause of the strike and made his report. I do not wish to be bound by what I say now, because my recollection of the facts may be astray. But, as I remember it, this report was to the effect that the strike ought not to have taken place. His verdict was against the strikers. It is hardly likely that both parties would be satisfied with the verdict, but I have reason to believe that some of the strikers have come to the conclusion that they were in the wrong, and that the report was justified. I think probably the report of the commission may incidentally explain the causes that led to the strike in Rossland. It was not necessary to go to Rossland, because peace had been restored, the parties were at work again, and a united effort was being made by both sides to revive the mining industry.' The commissioners thought that, under the circumstances it would be better not to go there and inquire into the causes of the trouble in Rossland. That was the decision of the commissioners in their wisdom, and I agree with it; it was not in the public interest to revive the feeling that existed so long between the parties.

That was the reason I asked the question. The Postmaster General has stated that when the strike took place in Rossland an invitation was extended to his department to send the deputy minister there, and he agreed to the request and sent the deputy minister. But what I wanted to know was why, when a strike took place in another part of the province, he did not send the deputy minister there rather than appoint a very expensive commission ?
I have given my explanation.

Did the hon. minister find that his department was unable to cope with the strike and the labour trouble? in British Columbia, and for that reason he was compelled to appoint this commission? While I am on myr feet, I wotilcl ask the hon. gentleman to answer the question where the request came from for the appointment of this commissison to investigate the labour troubles in British Columbia ?

The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) discusssed the subject with me and favoured the appointment of commissioners. Sc did Senator Templeman, a member of the government And they doubtless voiced the opinion of British Columbia to a considerable extent. I think my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Gallilier) also pressed it upon the consideration of the government, and, in fact, my recollection is that all the members from British Colum-

bia supporting the government expressed the same opinion.

And did not all the members opposing the government do the same ?
The rOSTMASTER GENERAL. I have no doubt my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes)-speaking now in all seriousness- if he has followed the reports in the press of the doings of this commission-will approve of the work that has been done, and will regard the commission as a very good thing for the province of British Columbia.

The Postmaster General did not answer the question put to him as to whether this commission was asked for by anybody. What strikes me is this : The Department of Labour costs us about $40,000 a year, and the amount of this vote is about one-third of that amount. Mr. King, I think, about doubled his salary for a considerable amount of time by this commission.
How ?
His salary, I believe, is $2,500. And on this commission he gets $5 a day and all expenses besides. I think that about amounts to doubling his salary.
Is that a fair statement?

I think it is. If it was necessary to take evidence to place before the House and the country in reference to the industrial position in British Columbia, it might have been done with far less expenditure. In fact, I do not see why Mr. King, if he is competent to till the position of Deputy Minister of Labour, could not have proceeded there. Commisssions of that kind have been issued and have taken evidence without so much expense to the country.
What instructions did the hon. minister give to the commissioners ? Did he direct what questions to ask ?

J may say to my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), also to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr Monk) and my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes), who have spoken, that, living as I do in British Columbia and in the mining districts where a number of these strikes have occurrred. in the coal mines, the gold mines and others, I may be permitted to say something on the necessity for such a commission as this. If these hon. gentlemen lived there as I do, and understood the conditions as I do, I do not think they would for a moment cavil at the government having appointed this commission rather than attempt to carry out the work by any single officer. This commission was given a very wide scope as to the taking of evidence and inquiry generally ; and, if
I may anticipate what the report of the commimssioners will be, I think members of the House will regard the appointment of the commission as in the interest of public peace generally and in the interest of trade generally, and will be thankful to the go\-ernment for appointing that commission to bring out these facts. I do not think that there is any way in which the work could have been so successfully done as by the means adopted by the government.
With regard to the strike in Rossland, some two years ago, I was in Nelson, not far from there, at the time Mr. King came out, and I may say that Mr. King did everything possible to bring about an understanding between the different parties. He met with some difficulty at the hands of the unions, and in fact was at first refused the privilege of interviewing the men generally upon the question. When it was afterwards suggested that they should discuss the matter and come to an arrangement, I am informed that the unions would not agree to be bound by any decision that was come to ; that while they were willing to submit the difficulty to investigation, they would not bind themselves to accept a verdict. Therefore, no fault could be found with Mr. King, because he did his duty as far as he was permitted to do it. A similar result might have occurred in the present case had that course been adopted. But as I say, the commission that has just sat were in a position to get at the root of the whole evil. I trust they have done so, and from the personnel of the men who compose that board of commissioners, I am satisfied they did do so. I think when their report is brought down a state of facts will be disclosed which will show that it was necessary to inquire into the power, if any, exercised by the western federation of miners or other organizations of the United States, over our unions in Canada. That certainly is a matter about which the people of Canada should have something to say, and in relation to which they should be in possession of the facts. If such power is detrimental to the interests of trade and the relations that should subsist between employer and employee in this country, the sooner the western federation of miners are cut off from exercising any control over our unions in Canada, the better for all concerned in Canada.
My hon. friend seems to find fault with us, and says that we are cavilling at the committee.

Not at all. I did not mean that. I think it is perfectly proper for members of the opposition to make themselves familiar with the reasons for the actions of the government, and they can only do so by questioning the minister.

We are not as well posted as the ministers, and we have to ask

for information in this way. But the hon. gentleman has gone too far when 'lie says that no fault was found with Mr. King, because fault was found with him.
By whom was the fault found ?
The minister has said by the union.
Some of the men, I do not know whether it was the union.

The minister has referred to the committee not sitting in Ross-land. That may have been a proper move for the commission to take. Rossland is certainly one of the most troublesome points in British Columbia as regards labour troubles.
All is quiet there now.

Here is a commission appointed for which the country has to pay, supposed to be composed of good sensible and competent men, and surely those interested in a matter of so much importance would find no fault in the commission sitting in Rossland to investigate the difficulties there because if they had gone to Rossland they would probably be in a better position to get evidence affecting the strikes in the past, and be able possibly to prevent them occurring in the future. However, I do not want to anticipate. I am willing to wait until the report is brought down, when we will have an opportunity of criticising the department and condemning it, if it deserves condemnation.
Amount required to meet expenses in connection with the commission to inquire into the Martineau defalcations. $1,100.
The three commissioners were Mr. Courtney, the deputy minister; Mr. Burn and Mr. Kent. The deputy minister receives no compensation. The report has been brought down.
Referring to the preceding item, did the minister say that the government instructed the commissioners where they were to hold their sittings, and that they were not to go to Rossland ?

The hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) asked what instructions were given to the commissioners. Their instructions were contained in the Order in Council appointing them, and required the commissioners to investigate the causes of the industrial and transportation troubles that have taken place in British Columbia. I think the commissioners were requested to sit at certain places, but well on towards the close of their sittings, the secretary of I Mr. INGRAM.
the commission telegraphed me to the effect that the commissioners thought it inexpedient in the public interest to go to Rossland, and left the matter in my hands to decide. I concurred with them in that view, and relieved them from going to Rossland. I do not think it would have been in the public interest to do so under the circumstances.
Would the minister give his reasons why he thought it was not in the interest of capital and labour that they should not sit at Rossland ?

Among the reasons set forth in the communication sent to me, one was that peace had been restored, and that it was not deemed expedient to bring the two parties, who had so recently been in hostility, into court again. There had been a long strike between employer and employee, and a great deal of trouble had been occasioned, loss of money, people had gone away, industry had suffered, and people were heartily sick of the trouble and wanted peace. It was thought that to bring these two hostile parties together again and inquire into the causes of their quarrel in the past, would have a bad effect, and would disturb the harmony that had been restored.
Grant to the Canadian South African Memorial Association, $6,000.

The object of this is to assist this association in marking the graves of Canadian soldiers who lost their lives in South Africa. The work has been undertaken by an association one of the chief members of which is Lady Minto. The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) is also one of its members, and I think that the military people generally are associated with it. They have raised by private subscription between $6,000 and $7,000 and they have askedl that the government should ' contribute. I am inclined to think that the government can do the work better in this way by co-operating with the association than ir we were to undertake it independently. The military people are giving a great deal of attention to the work, they have the cooperation of the military authorities in South Africa and as a result of this fund there will not be a grave of a Canadian soldier who lost his life in South Africa that will not be marked by a suitable monument.
The Dominion government assumes no control ?

No, we give them this grant the same as we would give it to any other organization.
To cover unprovided items, 1901-2, as per Auditor General's Report, page C-4, $200,635.65.

This is a formal item which the Auditor General desires to have passed at the end of the year to square his accounts. Where an appropriation is made for a department it sometimes happens that in one branch the appropriation is over expended, whereas in another branch there is an amount that is unused. Of course, the grants unused are greatly in excess of the over expenditures. The Auditor General likes to have this vote put into the Supply Bill. It is not really a vote of money, but it is rather a formal confirmation of the small over expenditures that have occurred during the year.
I was merely going to observe that it would have the effect of increasing the appropriation for a particular item.

As to a particular item it may be so, but the documents show that there are very large sums that are unused. Here aud there it is found impossible to keep the expenditure to the exact sum appropriated, and in sum cases by transfers from. one branch to another a readjustment takes place. This is not properly a vote of money, but it is simply to enable the Auditor General to square his accounts at the end of the year. I confess that for some years I had some difficulty in understanding why this was necessary, but it has been the practice of parliament for some years to vote an item of this character.
Scientific institutions and hydrographic surveys-amount required for time ball at Halifax N.S.. $1,000.

This time ball is erected at tlie request of the board of trade and the shipping interest at Halifax to give the mariners the time. The same thing exists at every ocean port. There is one at Montreal and also one at Quebec, maintained by the harbour commissioners. This is a new one and it is being erected under the supervision of Prof. Stupart, of the meteorological service.

Is this Captain MacGregor who used to sail on Lake Huron and Lake Superior ?
THE MINISTER OF MARINE' AND FISHERIES. Yes.

I think the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) wanted to say a word or two in regard to this*item not with the idea of objecting to it but he was rather inclined to think that some more liberal allowance should be made to this gentleman, who, I understand, has been twenty-seven years in the service of the country.
THE MINISTER OF MARINE AVD FISHERIES. Captain MacGregor is perfectly satisfied with this, and this is the ordinary gratuity.

I know nothing of the circumstances beyond what was mentioned to me by my hon. friend from North Grey. If the captain himself is perfectly satisfied with the allowance I would have nothing to say about it.
Is there not some rule that a month's salary shall be given for every year's service ?
That comes under the Superannuation Act. This Is not under the Superannuation Act.

Captain MacGregor is perfectly satisfied.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What will be the order of business for to-morrow ?

Several of the Bills and resolutions on the Paper may be reached, but we will move supply, the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) resuming consideration of his estimates. There are a number of scattered items yet which, if opportunity offers, will be brought forward. I would like myself to invite attention to the .supplementary estimates of the Railway Department, and if I can find time to-morrow to get the information they may be brought forward, but I doubt if I will have the time.
Is it the intention to take the resolutions with regard to bounties.

Possibly. My hon. friend had better assume that they may' be brought up. Perhaps there may be other business ahead, but if we do bring them up I would like my hon. friend to feel that he is not witnout notice.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12,55 a.m., Tuesday.
Tuesday, July 21, 1903.
